XRP ( CRYPTO: XRP ) initially reclaimed the number four spot in global crypto rankings in mid-March, overtaking BNB with a market cap of around $93 billion before the two assets traded places again. BNB reclaimed fourth briefly on March 23, reaching an $85.9 billion market cap versus XRP’s $85 billion, but the gap between the two remained under $1 billion. As of today, XRP is back at number four with a market cap of roughly $91 billion, rallying 10% to reach $1.50. The ranking battle with BNB is still on, but for now, XRP holds the edge, and the more interesting question is what comes next as the XRP price surges. The flip in March felt different, as that time, there were actual structural reasons behind it. On March 17, 2026, the SEC and CFTC issued joint guidance explicitly classifying XRP as a digital commodity. The practical effect was immediate: banks, hedge funds, and asset managers that had avoided XRP over the security question could now hold and trade it under the same commodity framework they already use for assets like gold and oil. XRP spiked to $1.60 on March 17 with trading volume surging roughly 250%, breaking out of the $1.35-to-$1.45 range. But the rally didn’t last as the Fed held rates the following day and raised its inflation forecast, dragging the entire crypto market down as a result. Then BNB briefly reclaimed fourth place on March 23 with an $85.9 billion market cap compared with XRP’s $85 billion, but the gap remained razor-thin, and XRP has now pulled back ahead. XRP’s ranking battle with BNB is essentially won for now, and the more interesting question is if XRP can close a gap three times larger and challenge Ethereum. Here are three key factors that could give XRP a shot at achieving such a feat. The CLARITY Act passed the House in July 2025 and is now targeting a Senate Banking Committee markup in the final two weeks of April. This is XRP’s biggest catalyst and could shape its price action for the rest of the year. The March commodity classification was a major step, but it was an interpretive release, which meant a future administration could revisit it. This means the CLARITY Act is what will make XRP’s regulatory status permanent. So, if it passes, it’ll give institutions the legal certainty they need to commit large capital to XRP. That alone could be a huge catalyst for XRP to close the gap on Ethereum in the global crypto rankings. There are currently six XRP ETFs in the U.S., but the breakdown of who holds them tells you a lot about where the upside is. Right now, roughly 84% of XRP ETF assets are held by retail investors, so only about 16% coming from institutions. Ripple has been expanding ODL corridors and signing new partners throughout 2025 and in 2026. The more payments that flow through XRP instead of traditional banking rails, the more consistent buying pressure builds under the price. If ODL volume scales from its current levels into the tens of billions annually, the demand could push XRP’s market cap closer to Ethereum’s. With XRP at $1.50 and a market cap of $91 billion, matching Ethereum’s current $295 billion valuation would require XRP to reach roughly $4.79—a 219% move from today’s price. That’s not impossible for XRP across a full cycle, but it’s a big ask in a single year that has already seen the token fall over 40% from its January high of $2.42. Catching Ethereum this year would need a near-perfect combination of the CLARITY Act passing , a macro recovery driving ETF inflows to multi-billion levels, and Ethereum continuing to trade below its prior highs. That’s a lot to line up at once. What’s more realistic for 2026 is XRP reaching $3.00-$4.00 to double in market cap—reaching roughly halfway to Ethereum. There are currently six XRP ETFs in the U.S., but the breakdown of who holds them tells you a lot about where the upside is. Right now, roughly 84% of XRP ETF assets are held by retail investors, so only about 16% coming from institutions.

Ripple has been expanding ODL corridors and signing new partners throughout 2025 and in 2026. The more payments that flow through XRP instead of traditional banking rails, the more consistent buying pressure builds under the price. If ODL volume scales from its current levels into the tens of billions annually, the demand could push XRP’s market cap closer to Ethereum’s.

With XRP at $1.50 and a market cap of $91 billion, matching Ethereum’s current $295 billion valuation would require XRP to reach roughly $4.79—a 219% move from today’s price. That’s not impossible for XRP across a full cycle, but it’s a big ask in a single year that has already seen the token fall over 40% from its January high of $2.42.

Catching Ethereum this year would need a near-perfect combination of the CLARITY Act passing , a macro recovery driving ETF inflows to multi-billion levels, and Ethereum continuing to trade below its prior highs. That’s a lot to line up at once. What’s more realistic for 2026 is XRP reaching $3.00-$4.00 to double in market cap—reaching roughly halfway to Ethereum.

XRP ( CRYPTO:XRP ) has seen a notable rise of 6.4% as of September 21, now trading at $1.47. This surge follows Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) breaking the $84,000 mark, rising 5.3% to $84,702—its highest point since January 31. Other cryptocurrencies are also riding the wave, with Ethereum up 5.4%, Solana surging 6.6%, and Zcash climbing 4.5%, contributing to a generally positive market.

XRP’s price surge is largely driven by Bitcoin, which forced exchanges to buy back around $300 million of losing short positions in just an hour. XRP had the largest share of shorts to unwind during this buying frenzy. However, despite the 6% jump, XRP is still down 1.5% over the past 30 days and about 20% for the year, so this daily gain hasn’t significantly changed its overall trend.

Bitcoin’s climb was the real trigger. Early in European trading on September 21, Bitcoin hovered around $82,000. As oil prices dipped and stock futures rose, it quickly shot to $84,700—a level it hadn’t seen in nearly eight months. As Bitcoin’s price rose, it reached levels where many short positions couldn’t maintain their margins, prompting exchanges to buy back coins at market prices to cover those positions. This process is known as short liquidation.

Simply put, when a trader shorts a coin, they borrow it and sell it, hoping to buy it back later at a lower price. But if the price increases and they can’t cover their losses, the exchange steps in to buy back the coin, driving the price up further. CoinGlass reported that in the hour Bitcoin crossed $84,000, about $313 million in positions were liquidated, with shorts making up 96% of that amount. Over 24 hours, around $710 million was liquidated, and shorts accounted for 86% of that total.

The forced buying helps all coins with significant short positions, but XRP stood out for a couple of reasons. First, XRP’s funding rate had been negative for over a week, meaning traders betting against XRP paid extra to hold their positions—indicating a crowded short market. Second, XRP had been lagging behind the market recently, causing traders who bet against it to accumulate large positions that became vulnerable during Bitcoin’s spike.

This helps explain why XRP gained 6.4% while Bitcoin rose 5.3%. Solana also rose 6.6%, partly due to its own upward trend before the squeeze. However, XRP’s rise this time was largely due to the positioning and the impact of Bitcoin’s movement.

Additionally, the 50-day moving average is rising and may soon cross above the 200-day average, a bullish signal known as a golden cross . However, once short positions are cleared, buying pressure may slow.

Probably not just from this alone. A short squeeze involves buying a cryptocurrency with money from other traders’ losses, and once those bets are closed, the buying stops. For XRP to stay at $1.47, Bitcoin needs to hold above $84,000 until regular buyers step in to replace those liquidations. However, Ripple has an upcoming event that could hurt this. On October 1, Ripple will release its monthly batch of one billion XRP from escrow, which usually doesn’t help the price in the days leading up to it.

So, why has XRP gone up? It’s largely because exchanges forced the liquidation of $300 million in short positions when Bitcoin broke $84,000, and XRP had the most crowded short positions among major cryptocurrencies. The downside is that no new buyers are supporting this price increase. If XRP closes above $1.50, it could target $1.55 and $1.70. Conversely, if it closes below $1.41, the squeeze pressure will be over, making $1.41 a key level to watch.

XRP shot up 60% in days and then collapsed 37% in a single minute, and the borrowed money that caused both moves is still sitting in the market. What that means for the next…

Two votes 24 hours apart, one in the Senate chamber and one from the Fed, will hit Bitcoin, XRP, Ethereum, and Solana differently, and only one of the four survives every possible combination without…
Solana just announced that XRP (CRYPTO: XRP) is live on its network—a move that connects two of crypto’s biggest ecosystems for the first time. XRP is now available on Solana as wXRP, a 1:1…
XRP surged past a stablecoin into fifth place on the crypto rankings after a move that had nothing to do with crypto fundamentals. The trigger came from the US Treasury, and it set off…

relevantPassages.text: Simply put, when a trader shorts a coin, they borrow it and sell it, hoping to buy it back later at a lower price.
But if the price increases and they can’t cover their losses, the exchange steps in to buy back the coin, driving the price up further.
CoinGlass reported that in the hour Bitcoin crossed $84,000, about $313 million in positions were liquidated, with shorts making up 96% of that amount.
Over 24 hours, around $710 million was liquidated, and shorts accounted for 86% of that total.
The downside is that no new buyers are supporting this price increase.
If XRP closes above $1.50, it could target $1.55 and $1.70.
Conversely, if it closes below $1.41, the squeeze pressure will be over, making $1.41 a key level to watch.
Sam Daodu is a crypto analyst who's spent nearly a decade making blockchain understandable—no easy task when most whitepapers read like fever dreams.
He writes for 24/7 Wall St., covering Bitcoin, altcoins, and crypto market analysis for investors.
Before crypto, he was a tech writer (back when explaining "the cloud" was peak innovation).
Since 2018, he's written for CoinTelegraph, Yahoo Finance, The Block, Cryptonews, Zypto, Rain, and more—basically anywhere people want crypto news without the headache.
Sam runs MacLabs Marketing, a content agency for crypto brands tired of sounding like AI wrote their website.
He also publishes free crypto education on his site for Web3 enthusiasts who think "gas fees" is a typo.

When he's not writing or staring at charts, Sam's either: - Watching anime (currently convinced One Piece has better tokenomics than most altcoins) - At the gym sculpting himself into a Greek god - Listening to the music your mum warned you only bad boys listen to Connect: LinkedIn | Email | MacLabs Marketing
XRP had the largest share of shorts to unwind during this buying frenzy.
However, despite the 6% jump, XRP is still down 1.5% over the past 30 days and about 20% for the year, so this daily gain hasn’t significantly changed its overall trend.
A short squeeze involves buying a cryptocurrency with money from other traders’ losses, and once those bets are closed, the buying stops.
For XRP to stay at $1.47, Bitcoin needs to hold above $84,000 until regular buyers step in to replace those liquidations.
However, Ripple has an upcoming event that could hurt this.
On October 1, Ripple will release its monthly batch of one billion XRP from escrow, which usually doesn’t help the price in the days leading up to it.
This surge follows Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) breaking the $84,000 mark, rising 5.3% to $84,702—its highest point since January 31.
Other cryptocurrencies are also riding the wave, with Ethereum up 5.4%, Solana surging 6.6%, and Zcash climbing 4.5%, contributing to a generally positive market.

passages: The Board has appointed independent director Mark N.
Schwartz to serve as Lead Independent Director, effective September 16, 2026.
Schwartz will help facilitate strong independent oversight of the Company while working closely with the Chairman and other members of the Board .
Schwartz is an accomplished CEO, CFO and board director with more than 36 years of leadership experience across the consumer, technology and healthcare sectors.

He co-founded Bodega Latina Corporation, which grew into a multibillion-dollar grocery business and the largest Hispanic retailer in the United States, led the IPO of DD Group plc and oversaw the sale of Bartell Drug Company to Rite Aid.

passages: Bitcoin was trading at $84,256 at around 06:35 a.m.
ET, up around 3.8%, according to CoinMetrics.
Earlier in the day, the cryptocurrency rose as high as $85,229, its highest level since late January.
Investors are assessing whether the "crypto winter" — a depressed period of digital asset prices — which began after bitcoin hit an all-time high of over $126,000 in October 2025, is over.
Bitcoin rose above $85,000 on Monday as the cryptocurrency continued its sharp rally over the past few days.
Analysts at BTIG said in a note on Sunday that, as long as the $75,000 level of bitcoin holds, "bulls can target a push through 82k on the way to" $90,000.
"I do think it's over, it's crypto spring, the crocuses are blooming," Matt Hougan, CIO at Bitwise, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday.
- CNBC's Tanaya Macheel and Garrett Downs contributed to this report.

"I do think it's over, it's crypto spring, the crocuses are blooming," Matt Hougan, CIO at Bitwise, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday. "I think this will actually be the strongest and longest-running bull market in crypto's history." While bitcoin is still down this year, it has risen more than 7% in the last 5 days and nearly 35% over the last 3 months. It is still well off its record high. Hougan said even though the market was down for a while, the "fundamentals went up" in cryptocurrency, pointing to more transactions across blockchains and involvement from major firms like BlackRock. "So I think we had this unusual situation where you had a cyclical decline in prices even as you had a secular improvement in fundamentals. And now I suspect that prices are going to catch up toward the end of the year," Hougan said. "I don't think if I came back next year, we'd still be below those all-time highs." Analysts at BTIG said in a note on Sunday that, as long as the $75,000 level of bitcoin holds, "bulls can target a push through 82k on the way to" $90,000. Crypto-related stocks, including Strategy and Coinbase , were higher in U.S. premarket trading on Monday. The rally comes even as the U.S. Senate last week blocked the Clarity Act from advancing. It would have set up a framework for crypto in the U.S. and divided industry oversight between the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). More regulation in the U.S., such as the Genius Act that was passed last year , has supported crypto prices. But the Clarity Act failing to pass could still boost prices, as the SEC and CFTC will set the rules for now, Hougan said. "It's the most pro-crypto SEC in the history of the U.S.; it's the most pro-crypto CFTC in the history of the U.S. So ironically, in the absence of Clarity passing, we may actually have stronger pro-crypto regulation," Hougan said. The Bitwise CIO also said that investors are rotating out of AI stocks back into crypto. He added that the AI boom had "sucked all the oxygen out of the room. Any investor who was a momentum-driven investor was focused on that. Now that that has sort of levelled off, you're seeing that money rotate back into crypto." - CNBC's Tanaya Macheel and Garrett Downs contributed to this report. Got a confidential news tip? sources.title: World model companies are keeping a lot of secrets

extraction.body: This week, I moderated a panel on world models at the All In conference (no relation to the podcast), and it gave me a chance to dig into one of the most mysterious corners of the AI world. The big players in the space are Yann LeCun’s AMI Labs and Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs — and while both have accumulated a lot of buzz and funding, they also rank pretty low on the trying-to-make-money scale . At their core, world models are about automating spatial intelligence , so the field could head in lots of exciting and lucrative directions, from robotics to interactive video to more complex self-driving systems. But when I started to press on where we would actually see the tech commercialized, things got foggy. The closest thing I found to an authority was Michael Rabbat, a co-founder of AMI Labs and the company’s VP of World Models, who joined me on the panel. But when I pressed him on exactly what the company was working on, he was cagey. “We’ll talk about it when we’re ready to talk about it.” Over email, he clarified, “We’re still in a research and building phase, so we’re not talking publicly about any product plans or timeline.” To be fair, AMI is less than a year old, so it’s fair enough to keep quiet. But this sort of caginess extends to the whole world-modeling space. World Labs’ Marble is probably the most fully developed product in the space, and its demos range from straightforward media creation, building explorable environments for video games, or CGI effects. There are robotics use cases too, but the whole platform seems more designed to demonstrate capabilities. That secrecy even extends to these companies’ suppliers. On the sidelines of the same conference, I spoke to Alex de Vigan, CEO of Physicl — a data supplier for the burgeoning world model business. He says he knows Physicl’s data has been useful for whatever they’re building, but he’s still in the dark about what exactly that is. “I wish they would tell us more. We could build more useful data if we knew what they were working on,” de Vigan told me. Part of the mystery comes from how versatile world models are as an idea. The simplest version is a navigable map of the world, similar to the AI models that power self-driving cars. But the same modeling approach that helps a Waymo weave through traffic could also help a humanoid robot carry boxes, or turn a few minutes of video footage into an explorable environment. AMI has already dipped its toe in manufacturing, biomedicine, robotics, and even AI software for doctors through its Nabia partnership. Surely it won’t pursue all of those — but maybe one or two of them are standing out? No one doubts that there are lots of viable businesses to be built on world model tech — and as long as it’s easy to fundraise, there’s no particular pressure to focus on one. In fact, there’s good reason not to. If AMI announced tomorrow that they had built a humanoid OpenClaw or a next-generation Hollywood rendering system, a lot of other labs would suddenly be very interested in the space. Soon, the lab would face potential competition from the other world model companies, the neolabs, and even OpenAI and Anthropic. In some ways, it’s the flip side of all that easy fundraising. Your competitors can fundraise, too — and the same money that lets you build under the radar is also funding lots of potential rivals once the path to market becomes clear. But even if that competition is inevitable, it’s best if you delay it for as long as possible, which means keeping quiet about exactly what you’re building. Cixin Liu fans will recognize this as a dark forest scenario : If you don’t know who else is in the woods, it’s best not to attract attention. I will say, I don’t think I was completely wrong, because even with these loose plans that Dario laid out in a blog post and and some of the other leaders have talked about, I feel like we’re still missing a lot of specifics here, not only on some of the claims about why these people think there are dangers and risks, but also specifics on what they mean by slowing down.

extraction.body: We’re seeing a big debate over AI safety and a potential slowdown, as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently published a plan to “pace the frontier,” while Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has publicly echoed President Donald Trump’s claims that the AI backlash is a hoax and regulation is unnecessary. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed whether executives like Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman are serious about wanting to slow down. While I was surprised at how many industry leaders seemed to throw their support behind Amodei’s plan, Sean noted that the plan seemed short on details. And when Kristen asked whether a combination of existing regulation and the workings of the free market could provide enough safeguards on their own, Sean replied, “We have a federal government at the moment that certainly does not seem eager to enforce regulations broadly speaking, let alone specifically speaking here.” Plus, he argued, “There does not seem like there is a ton of consumer choice driving this market, in the sense of, okay, if one of these companies does something really bad, then they will see an impact in how many cancellations there are or whatever.” Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Anthony Ha: Sean, what do you think? Are we actually going to”‘pace the frontier”? Sean O’Kane: That sounds, for some reason, like something from “Point Break.” It’s just a very California statement, like, “We’re gonna pace the frontier, bruh.” I don’t know. I said on this show last week , I didn’t think we were headed for a slowdown of any kind, in large part because I don’t think these companies are structured in a way where that works. So this was a pretty immediate flip of what I said a week ago, to hear this from Dario at Anthropic and Sam at OpenAI and even Elon Musk to a certain degree — and we can get into whether we believe that or not. I will say, I don’t think I was completely wrong, because even with these loose plans that Dario laid out in a blog post and and some of the other leaders have talked about, I feel like we’re still missing a lot of specifics here, not only on some of the claims about why these people think there are dangers and risks, but also specifics on what they mean by slowing down. Anthony, I know you read this stuff pretty closely last weekend as it was all popping off, so I’m curious if you’re maybe more generous than I am, as far as understanding what it is they’re trying to say here. Anthony: I mean, I also have questions. What really stood out to me is the fact that so many people in the industry seemed to coalesce around this fairly quickly. Even before Amodei published his blog post, I was seeing other people post some version of this [plan,] just in the days leading up to it. My understanding is, these suggestions that have come out of the AI safety community; these are things that have been percolating for a while. They’re not just things that [Amodei] thought up on his own. But it just seemed like a lot of people were kind of ready to embrace this and in some ways, [it’s] encouraging to see that there’s a consensus. But it also makes me a little skeptical that this would represent genuine, major steps towards a slowdown. Kirsten Korosec: First of all, consensus can be a good thing. Also, it can be the beginnings of forming a cartel. And so, let’s be clear [about] who we’re talking about here. We’re talking about frontier AI labs. and that’s specific and important. You did say a minute ago that the details aren’t really clear, but we do know that the general idea here is that independent third party evaluators would come in that would work inside [companies] like Anthropic or OpenAI and monitor AI safety practices and incidents. But there is a lot of vagueness around that. Then there’s another proposal to have major AI companies in democratic countries coordinate on safety standards and limits. And then this international coordination piece. So those are the general ideas around this. I’ll also add that there’s been very considerable pushback from very specific people. And surprisingly, some people I didn’t think would push back on this. The obvious one, I guess, would be Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang, who had some pretty choice words. I don’t know what either of you think of […] some of his comments and the call he took from President Trump on-stage [at the All-In Summit] Sean: I think Jensen understands that, to a certain extent, he is seen as the adult in the room here. Which is interesting, because that’s a dynamic that I think has changed. If you were to ask people a year, almost two years ago now, who was playing that role as these AI companies were really starting to blow up in big ways, I think a lot of people would have pointed to Microsoft and Satya Nadella, and I feel like Microsoft has — for a number of reasons that we don’t need to get into right now — lost that grip on being the adult in the room. Certainly in part because Nadella said he was going to make Google dance , and then that never happened. and in fact, the opposite happened, in a lot of ways. Jensen, I think, understands not only that he needs to be pleasing the most amount of people and so he wants to say the most measured thing, he also is one of the most useful liaisons between this field and this administration, to the point that he’s getting a call from the president while he’s on-stage at this very well-attended and high-profile conference that allowed both of them to respond to all this mess. Kirsten: [To] your point about him being the adult in the room and the liaison, he is in a position where he could do that. But in my view, I would say that [his appearance,] which did feel a little staged, went a step too far and really highlighted the fact that Nvidia greatly benefits from AI moving forward in an unpaced manner. I hate to be cynical about it, but that was sort of my initial reaction to it. Anthony: Trump’s and Huang’s interests are aligned, and also [Huang’s] telling [Trump] what he wants to hear. I did think some of the things he was specifically focusing on are worth unpacking a little bit. First he talked about this idea of, “We are not going to have a slowdown.” It’s interesting, just that phrase “slowdown,” which has come up a lot — but at the same time, both Altman and Amade [will] use the slowdown language, but the word they like to use more is “pace.” right? And these three proposals — the ones you just described, Kirsten — in theory, they could result in things slowing down, but they’re not saying that explicitly. It’s saying, “Hey, we’re making some basic safety measures and having some people keep an eye on us.” But none of those things are intrinsically saying that things have to go slower than they are now, at least as I understand it. Kirsten: So I have a question for Sean. Couldn’t you argue in a free market society, we have existing regulations in place, and also [in] the competitive environment in which there isn’t protectionism, if there is something unsafe that is released by a company, that they would no longer be able to be a viable company? And there are regulators in place today that could go after these companies? Or do you reject that idea? Sean: In a vacuum, or in a market that is not being distorted by a whole bunch of different external pressures, yeah, I think there’s an element of that. But we have a federal government at the moment that certainly does not seem eager to enforce regulations broadly speaking, let alone specifically speaking here. And we’re also in this weird situation where — I don’t really know the right way to put it, but it does not seem like there is a ton of consumer choice driving this market, in the sense of, okay, if one of these companies does something really bad, then they will see an impact in how many cancellations there are or whatever. Especially now, as they have moved into enterprise and they’re making so much more of their money from selling their services to companies, it’s just naturally harder to vote with your dollars there. Corporations are not going to pack up and move from [OpenAI’s] Codex to [Anthropic’s] Claude Code just because they disagree on principle with something that OpenAI did. And then they’re also just being floated by so much investment money that it makes it easier for them to absorb any of those losses if they actually do face them. So I think it’s a nice idea in theory, but I feel like in practice, there’s none of that really happening. The obvious one, I guess, would be Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang, who had some pretty choice words. passages: iFixit’s latest device teardown shows us the inner workings of the new variable aperture lens inside Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, alongside some repair concerns to be mindful of.

extraction.body: iFixit’s latest device teardown shows us the inner workings of the new variable aperture lens inside Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, alongside some repair concerns to be mindful of. The adjustable mechanical iris opens and closes magnetically, controlling how much light should pass through to the sensor, featuring six leaf-like overlapping blades that are each about as thin as a human hair. Doing so would require specialist tools, techniques, and knowledge that few people possess, making this as close to “impossible” to repair as it gets, according to iFixit. That means users will likely have to replace the entire camera assembly, which is thankfully easy to access.

The adjustable mechanical iris opens and closes magnetically, controlling how much light should pass through to the sensor, featuring six leaf-like overlapping blades that are each about as thin as a human hair. Doing so would require specialist tools, techniques, and knowledge that few people possess, making this as close to “impossible” to repair as it gets, according to iFixit. That means users will likely have to replace the entire camera assembly, which is thankfully easy to access.

sources.body: Crucially, the panel says the world does not need to wait for scientists to establish exactly how or why such incidents occur to begin implementing stronger safeguards.

extraction.body: Governments need to rein in increasingly capable AI agents before their risks are fully understood, a United Nations scientific panel warned in the global organization’s first major assessment of OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face earlier this year. Last week, UN secretary general António Guterres called on governments to cooperate on addressing the threats posed by AI, warning that “the world cannot afford a race to the bottom on AI safety.” It is the first thematic brief from the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, established last year as the UN’s “first global scientific body on Artificial Intelligence.” It calls for much greater attention and resources to manage emerging risks from advanced AI, alongside stronger international coordination on safety and accountability, even as individual countries take different legal approaches. Crucially, the panel says the world does not need to wait for scientists to establish exactly how or why such incidents occur to begin implementing stronger safeguards. Loss-of-control risk, the panel argues, is exactly the kind of problem the precautionary principle was designed to address: “one where potential harm may be catastrophic or irreversible, even as its likelihood remains scientifically uncertain.” The principle, first enshrined in the 1992 UN Rio Declaration on Environment and Development, says that scientific uncertainty is no excuse for delaying measures against potentially serious or irreversible harm. It has since become influential in environmental and public health policy, particularly in the European Union. Since the Hugging Face hack was first reported, incidents have been documented at companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta, including hacks on real-world targets and swarms of agents taking over online messaging boards.

sources.title: Amazon doesn’t trust Meta’s Muse AI agent
passages: Meta’s Muse AI agent has been blocked from shopping Amazon on behalf of its users, GeekWire reports.

A popup message started appearing on Sunday for Muse users saying that “continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use, to which our customers have agreed.” According to GeekWire, Meta didn’t notify Amazon that Muse would access its store.
When Meta launched Muse earlier this month, it said the AI agent cannot see secure login details or card payment information.
Amazon also expressed privacy and security concerns over Muse failing to identify itself when it browses, and seemingly capturing customer credentials.

Confirmation emails from Amazon have also started looking notably sparse since July, with specific item names and product images being omitted to limit that information from being mined by external AI services.
We used it during testing to successfully purchase tank tops from Amazon while other products were in the basket.
This marks Amazon’s latest effort to fend off competition from rival agentic AI services and keep its customers shopping with the retailer directly.

It sued Perplexity in November last year in a similar attempt to keep the Amazon platform out of the AI search provider’s Comet shopping experience, with a judge siding with Perplexity on the case in August.

Virtually every one is some kind of faceless alabaster humanoid with no details of note, and some are mere rehashes of past favorites, such as the fleshy straight-jacketed figure, although this time it has a plank driven through its head. Zoe, on the other hand, is saddled with a pager, a far less effective item since it doesn’t directly reveal enemy movements. Instead, bars around the sides fill up to show their approximate direction and proximity. Both gadgets, though, are effective at grounding Townfall in the real world. At certain points, the CRTV can be tuned to show recorded messages that help develop the story or provide hints. The pager, meanwhile, receives mission- and story-related communication. Usually, it’s something obscure and surreal, such as interacting with a well or a red square on a wall, but here you use landlines (no mobile phones in St. Amelia 1996) and dial 100 — the in-game number for the coastguard. There’s little beyond the main objectives at hand to seek out, aside from some mysterious coded postcards that’ll have fans scrabbling to decipher, as well as hidden phone numbers to find. There are also unlockable outfits and weapons, and five different endings to get. Townfall isn’t particularly scary. There’s the occasional jump scare, but it doesn’t rely on them for cheap thrills. The game is a slow burn, with plenty of quiet, contemplative moments as you explore your surroundings. As with many Silent Hill games, the horror is more psychological. But herein lies a problem. While the story is commendable for sustaining the mystery for as long as possible, there’s a lack of character exploration, contrary to many other stories in the franchise. The characters’ dialogue is mostly cryptic, so you never get much of a grasp on their thoughts and feelings until the end — and even then, there are still plenty of questions left unanswered, as they should be. But the three of them are by turns confused and forlorn throughout. This mixture works to conjure that strange, uncanny tone the series is known for, but it also means the trio fails to elicit the same level of emotional investment garnered by past protagonists, such as Harry and Heather Mason, James Sunderland, and Mary. Social commentary seems to be Townfall’s primary concern: the main theme is one of corporate negligence and its devastating impact on a community, which is certainly relevant in today’s world. And it’s true that once the three collide and everything comes to a head, it starts to resonate emotionally. But this is a long time coming, and Zoe ultimately feels underserved by the story’s conclusion, a shame given the aforementioned excellence of her actor’s performance. It’s entirely possible, though, that other endings will give her a larger role than the one I reached, although I have no idea how these are achieved yet. Ultimately, I found Townfall less impactful than Silent Hill 2 or Shattered Memories . You want great art direction Screen Burn has managed to haul a small Scottish fishing village into the world of Silent Hill beautifully. It looks and sounds fantastic. You want the best monsters The monsters are certainly less memorable this time round, a shame given the series’ pedigree in this area. You want more emotion from your characters Mostly, the three protagonists are quite stilted in their tone. The botoxed facial animations don’t help, either. There are no content filters for blood and gore, and visual assists for color and contrast, and the like, are also missing. You can toggle subtitles and closed captions separately, though, and you can adjust the opacity of their backgrounds. There are three difficulty modes to choose from: Story, which reduces the threat posed by enemies; Normal, which is how the developers intend the game to be played; and Nightmare, which increases enemy power and makes your flashlight detectable by them. I played the game on a standard PS5, largely in Performance mode, although I also tested Quality mode for a time, too. I used a Lenovo Legion R27qe monitor and the Skullcandy Crusher PLYR 720 headset for audio.

What is it? A single-player psychological horror game which takes place on an isolated Scottish island. The protagonist Simon Ordell has to solve puzzles, fight monsters, and figure out what the hell is going on. Release date September 24, 2026 Expect to pay $50 / £45 Developer Screen Burn Publisher Konami Reviewed on RTX 3070, Core AMD Ryzen 5 5600G, 16GB RAM Multiplayer No Steam Deck Unknown Link Steam Walking up to the old town of St Amelia for the first time in Silent Hill: Townfall, I was greeted by that familiar thick fog and eerie quiet—an omen of the horrors to come. I know what kind of monsters are waiting for me beyond the fog and I am painfully aware of just how unprepared I am for it—with no flashlight, healing items, or weapon on hand. But weirdly enough none of that matters, because for the first time in a Silent Hill game I feel content. St Amelia is a fictional town, but as I'm sure many players based in the UK will soon discover, developer Screen Burn breathes so much life into this sleepy fishing village that I could've sworn I'd been here before. It's certainly a strange feeling to have in a game like this, but with Konami opening Silent Hill up to the world it's now the UK's turn to have our sense of home toyed with. The story follows Simon Ordell, a man unknown to us and himself. The only sense of person he has comes from a medical bracelet with his name, date of birth, and blood type written on it. I watched as he dragged himself up from the waves of the North Sea, onto the docks, and headed into St Amelia seeking help and answers as to why he's here on this cold foggy island. A Silent Hill game is nothing without its setting and St Amelia delivers. I spent more time than I'd care to admit reading info boards about the history of fishing on the island and peeping over fences to see how the locals had done up their gardens. The more I explored, the better sense I got of the kind of people who lived in this town and what had happened to them. Simon also sees more than just the old town as he ventures to a hospital, a corporate office, your classic Silent Hill supernatural 'other place', and, brace yourself, some new builds. My time in St Amelia flew by rather quickly, with just 13 hours spent in total, but that was more than enough to be rewarded with heaps of brilliant visual storytelling and the usual gift of stressful encounters. St Amelia has its fair share of gut-wrenching horrors lurking around each corner, though—you don't spend a grand total of 35 minutes and five seconds hiding in lockers unless there's something pretty bad waiting for you on the other side. But even still, I found myself drawn to exploring the fog because my curiosity outweighed my fear. But the further I progressed the less content I became. Not because there were more faceless and bound monsters stumbling around (although that didn't help), but because there was more to the island than St Amelia's historic old town. There was a side that was painfully familiar—cobblestone streets shifted into tarmac roads and cottages were turned into flats for better efficiency. The island changed as Simon moved away from the heart of St Amelia and towards the parasite which had latched onto it. Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team. The town itself felt alive more than just lived in, and if that doesn't tick all the boxes for a world-class Silent Hill setting, I don't know what does. A good rule of thumb in Silent Hill is to approach its puzzles with lateral thinking, and Townfall is no different. They start fairly easy, coaching you in the art of taking in absolutely everything from your surroundings, digesting it, and then stitching together an answer from what has been gathered. It's the classic case of finding the combination to a lock by sifting through letters conveniently left scattered around the near vicinity. But as I spent more time in St Amelia, my brain gradually got the hang of looking at things from a Silent Hill perspective. And although the puzzles got harder it didn't feel like a noticeable difference. Hell, the first thing I thought when stumbling across a bunch of blood types scribbled across the wall was "This is a puzzle and it wants me to figure out how to create blood type A+". If it weren't for the 7+ hours I'd already spent in Townfall I doubt that would have been my default response. There were a few exceptions towards the very end of the game, however, I think a fresh brain would have had far less issues. Take the dreaded pipe room for example, where I had to use what looked to be morse code to twist a room full of levers in the right direction. After bashing my head against my desk my synapses sparked, a thought was formed, and I figured it out—I wish you all the best of luck with that one. The puzzles aren't the only smart design features in Townfall, though, with the best and brightest being the handheld CRTV. This quickly became my closest companion as it allowed me to see the creepies through any wall or obstacle. It may seem like a bit of a cheat code getting to know where the monsters are but there are some limitations. The CRTV may be the most creative, fun, and useful puzzle solving tool I've ever had the pleasure of playing with. I wouldn't say I'm much of a pacifist but I opted to forgo the planks of wood, pipes, and firearms for most of the game, instead favouring the CRTV as my weapon against the monsters to help me stealth around them. I played on the normal difficulty and I didn't have a run in with a monster until quite far into the latter stages of the game. They're not blind, I was just able to move around them with some ease if I used the CRTV correctly and was cautiously optimistic about how fast Simon could run. Even with all its finicky buttons the CRTV may be the most creative, fun, and useful puzzle solving tool I've ever had the pleasure of playing with. It turned navigating Townfall into one big scary puzzle, which is exactly what I look for in Silent Hill. But all of these amazing puzzles and fantastic world building would be for nought if Townfall hadn't also been able to pull off the kind of beautiful and psychologically jarring storytelling we've come to expect from the Silent Hill series. But the fact that there's something off about Simon isn't what interests me—the fun part is finding out what he did. To say there's something wrong with Simon would be to state the obvious. We're in a Silent Hill game after all, and no one in their sound mind would hallucinate grotesque faceless monsters which shoot needles out from their abdomens. But the fact that there's something off about Simon isn't what interests me—the fun part is finding out what he did to end up like this. It's clear that people in the town are angry, that some awful disaster happened on this island which rocked its community to its core. What's unclear, however, is why it involves some seemingly random American dude with induced amnesia. But Simon's not on his own. There are two other characters who also inhabit this liminal space with him—Zoe and Richard. At first I just thought these to be your typical filler characters but as it turns out these two are perhaps the most interesting characters to have ever fallen into the fog. My favourite sequence in all of Townfall was actually Zoe's part. In this she relives the aftermath of the disaster as a nurse and a first responder to the victims as she tries to save the life of an unknown patient. I am not a trained nurse so taking the patient's readings, running tests, and ultimately medicating them was probably one of the more stressful experiences I've had in a horror game. But it was worth it because through the stress I understood her guilt and trauma with painful clarity. It also made it clear why she's found herself wrapped up in this mess. Then there's Richard who is an opposite to Zoe in every sense of the word. He's not blameless or caring; he's an asshole. But boy, is he an interesting character study. I won't go into too much detail concerning Richard as his story is one that is better experienced firsthand. But, like with Zoe, after playing through his sequence it became clear to me what this game's curse is. While the answer seemed simple at first examining the curse through the lens of three different characters adds enough diversity for an incredibly rewarding story and analysis of its characters. My only issue with Townfall was that I didn't get to spend more time with Zoe and Richard, because in comparison Simon is just a little boring. His role as a blank template for players to print themselves onto worked wonders for immersion but ultimately his character suffered for it. I found myself drawn more to Zoe and Richard, two characters who had more invested in this community from the get go. That's not to say I dislike Simon. He's a fantastic character who comes into his own during the latter stages of the story and is someone who will grow on me the more time I spend mulling Townfall over. After all was said and done and I'd finally reached the end of Townfall's brilliant story, my overwhelming feeling was one of relief. Like Silent Hill f before it, Townfall had some monumental expectations to live up to and the unenviable task of proving that yet again the mystique of Silent Hill is not limited to one mountainous town. But it's now clear that Screen Burn absolutely understands what makes a great Silent Hill game and the series is better off for it. 2026 games : All the upcoming games Best PC games : Our all-time favorites Free PC games : Freebie fest Best FPS games : Finest gunplay Best RPGs : Grand adventures Best co-op games : Better together Silent Hill: Townfall is just the right mix of old and new. But weirdly enough none of that matters, because for the first time in a Silent Hill game I feel content.

St Amelia is a fictional town, but as I'm sure many players based in the UK will soon discover, developer Screen Burn breathes so much life into this sleepy fishing village that I could've sworn I'd been here before. It's certainly a strange feeling to have in a game like this, but with Konami opening Silent Hill up to the world it's now the UK's turn to have our sense of home toyed with.

The story follows Simon Ordell, a man unknown to us and himself. The only sense of person he has comes from a medical bracelet with his name, date of birth, and blood type written on it. I watched as he dragged himself up from the waves of the North Sea, onto the docks, and headed into St Amelia seeking help and answers as to why he's here on this cold foggy island.

A Silent Hill game is nothing without its setting and St Amelia delivers. I spent more time than I'd care to admit reading info boards about the history of fishing on the island and peeping over fences to see how the locals had done up their gardens. The more I explored, the better sense I got of the kind of people who lived in this town and what had happened to them.

Simon also sees more than just the old town as he ventures to a hospital, a corporate office, your classic Silent Hill supernatural 'other place', and, brace yourself, some new builds. My time in St Amelia flew by rather quickly, with just 13 hours spent in total, but that was more than enough to be rewarded with heaps of brilliant visual storytelling and the usual gift of stressful encounters.

St Amelia has its fair share of gut-wrenching horrors lurking around each corner, though—you don't spend a grand total of 35 minutes and five seconds hiding in lockers unless there's something pretty bad waiting for you on the other side. But even still, I found myself drawn to exploring the fog because my curiosity outweighed my fear.

But the further I progressed the less content I became. Not because there were more faceless and bound monsters stumbling around (although that didn't help), but because there was more to the island than St Amelia's historic old town. There was a side that was painfully familiar—cobblestone streets shifted into tarmac roads and cottages were turned into flats for better efficiency. The island changed as Simon moved away from the heart of St Amelia and towards the parasite which had latched onto it.

The town itself felt alive more than just lived in, and if that doesn't tick all the boxes for a world-class Silent Hill setting, I don't know what does.

A good rule of thumb in Silent Hill is to approach its puzzles with lateral thinking, and Townfall is no different. They start fairly easy, coaching you in the art of taking in absolutely everything from your surroundings, digesting it, and then stitching together an answer from what has been gathered. It's the classic case of finding the combination to a lock by sifting through letters conveniently left scattered around the near vicinity.

But as I spent more time in St Amelia, my brain gradually got the hang of looking at things from a Silent Hill perspective. And although the puzzles got harder it didn't feel like a noticeable difference. Hell, the first thing I thought when stumbling across a bunch of blood types scribbled across the wall was "This is a puzzle and it wants me to figure out how to create blood type A+". If it weren't for the 7+ hours I'd already spent in Townfall I doubt that would have been my default response.

There were a few exceptions towards the very end of the game, however, I think a fresh brain would have had far less issues. Take the dreaded pipe room for example, where I had to use what looked to be morse code to twist a room full of levers in the right direction. After bashing my head against my desk my synapses sparked, a thought was formed, and I figured it out—I wish you all the best of luck with that one.

The puzzles aren't the only smart design features in Townfall, though, with the best and brightest being the handheld CRTV. This quickly became my closest companion as it allowed me to see the creepies through any wall or obstacle. It may seem like a bit of a cheat code getting to know where the monsters are but there are some limitations.
The CRTV may be the most creative, fun, and useful puzzle solving tool I've ever had the pleasure of playing with.

I wouldn't say I'm much of a pacifist but I opted to forgo the planks of wood, pipes, and firearms for most of the game, instead favouring the CRTV as my weapon against the monsters to help me stealth around them. I played on the normal difficulty and I didn't have a run in with a monster until quite far into the latter stages of the game. They're not blind, I was just able to move around them with some ease if I used the CRTV correctly and was cautiously optimistic about how fast Simon could run.

Even with all its finicky buttons the CRTV may be the most creative, fun, and useful puzzle solving tool I've ever had the pleasure of playing with. It turned navigating Townfall into one big scary puzzle, which is exactly what I look for in Silent Hill.

But all of these amazing puzzles and fantastic world building would be for nought if Townfall hadn't also been able to pull off the kind of beautiful and psychologically jarring storytelling we've come to expect from the Silent Hill series.
But the fact that there's something off about Simon isn't what interests me—the fun part is finding out what he did.

To say there's something wrong with Simon would be to state the obvious. We're in a Silent Hill game after all, and no one in their sound mind would hallucinate grotesque faceless monsters which shoot needles out from their abdomens. But the fact that there's something off about Simon isn't what interests me—the fun part is finding out what he did to end up like this. It's clear that people in the town are angry, that some awful disaster happened on this island which rocked its community to its core. What's unclear, however, is why it involves some seemingly random American dude with induced amnesia.

But Simon's not on his own. There are two other characters who also inhabit this liminal space with him—Zoe and Richard. At first I just thought these to be your typical filler characters but as it turns out these two are perhaps the most interesting characters to have ever fallen into the fog.

My favourite sequence in all of Townfall was actually Zoe's part. In this she relives the aftermath of the disaster as a nurse and a first responder to the victims as she tries to save the life of an unknown patient.

I am not a trained nurse so taking the patient's readings, running tests, and ultimately medicating them was probably one of the more stressful experiences I've had in a horror game. But it was worth it because through the stress I understood her guilt and trauma with painful clarity. It also made it clear why she's found herself wrapped up in this mess.

Then there's Richard who is an opposite to Zoe in every sense of the word. He's not blameless or caring; he's an asshole. But boy, is he an interesting character study. I won't go into too much detail concerning Richard as his story is one that is better experienced firsthand. But, like with Zoe, after playing through his sequence it became clear to me what this game's curse is. While the answer seemed simple at first examining the curse through the lens of three different characters adds enough diversity for an incredibly rewarding story and analysis of its characters.

My only issue with Townfall was that I didn't get to spend more time with Zoe and Richard, because in comparison Simon is just a little boring. His role as a blank template for players to print themselves onto worked wonders for immersion but ultimately his character suffered for it. I found myself drawn more to Zoe and Richard, two characters who had more invested in this community from the get go.

That's not to say I dislike Simon. He's a fantastic character who comes into his own during the latter stages of the story and is someone who will grow on me the more time I spend mulling Townfall over.

After all was said and done and I'd finally reached the end of Townfall's brilliant story, my overwhelming feeling was one of relief. Like Silent Hill f before it, Townfall had some monumental expectations to live up to and the unenviable task of proving that yet again the mystique of Silent Hill is not limited to one mountainous town. But it's now clear that Screen Burn absolutely understands what makes a great Silent Hill game and the series is better off for it.

extraction.body: The Silent Hill franchise is having a resurgence, and I’m all for it. With 3 straight autumns of new releases: Silent Hill 2 Remake, Silent Hill f, and now Silent Hill: Townfall, fans are in for a treat with this new rendition. After playing through all 3, I’m genuinely impressed with how much each individual title stands out from one another. Screen Burn has done an incredible job crafting their own version of Silent Hill, and Townfall might be the best one yet. I was initially worried after my hands-on preview that Townfall might be a rehash of Silent Hill 2, but boy was I wrong. Screen Burn wasn’t lying when they said the game would be social commentary around big corporations, coverups, and whistleblowers. The narrative truly does deliver here, and with several endings to achieve, I’ll have to see them all to get the full picture of the story and message. Pacing is also excellent, with the overall length of the gaming feeling just right, not too short, and not too long. If you want a brief refresher on what the game is, check out my preview. You do get to step into the perspective of other characters, Zoe and Richard. All of them have ties to one another in some way. Not only does this allow you to see a different side of the narrative, piecing together things that were confusing to you before, but it also forces you to play a bit differently than Simon. Zoe starts off with absolutely nothing other than a pager, meaning she doesn’t have the CRTV to help locate threats or a melee weapon to defend herself. You have to rely on pure stealth to pass her sections. Richard, on the other hand, starts off with a shotgun, and the game absolutely showers you with ammo, so feel free to go to town with anything that comes your way. The “survival horror” gameplay might not break the typical mold of the genre, but Townfall does so with confidence and grace. Why fix what ain’t broke right? Ammunition is scarce, melee weapons like wooden sticks and pipes degrade and break, and healing items can be crafted to create better ones. The only real new additions are Simon’s CRTV and his IV bag that acts as a second life if he is fatally struck. You’ll be switching between pure stealth sections and hybrid stealth and combat portions, and the cadence and transitions help it not to feel forced or weird. The Alien Isolation influence is seen clearly, with several spaces to hide in, radios to turn on to draw attention, and bottles and bricks to throw to distract. Gunplay, on the other hand, is crisp and responsive, and for the revolver, you can physically see yourself reloading all 6 bullets into the chamber before you can fire again. Simon gets his hands on a flare gun later in the game too. The gameplay and narrative sail smoothly into one another in a way that feels like natural progression. My only complaint is that some forced stealth sections are a bit too dragged out. In the middle chapter of the game, there is a Mr. X-like entity that is unkillable and will one-shot you if you’re caught. These sections last a bit too long for my liking. The enemy AI is a tad too sensitive, so any small movement will trigger them, forcing you to hide and de-aggro them. Normally immense backtracking would be a point of contention with horror titles, but Townfall strikes a good balance at this. You’re never really treading the same path more than a couple times, and levels are intricately designed so that you might find a new path to a previously visited area. This is also true when you play as different characters, so don’t worry about them tasking you to do the same thing twice. This is not a game that holds your hand, even on “Hinted” difficulty for puzzles. You’ll have to think outside the box or even brute force some solutions if you can’t figure them out. That being said, I absolutely adored the variety of riddles that range from your typical image alignment with the CRTV all the way to more complex ones that require you to keep track of several key factors and backtrack to previously inaccessible areas. My favorite involved finding blood bags of different patients and piecing together their blood types. There were ones that veered on the edge of being too obscure, so take that as you will. Like I mentioned in my preview, these brainteasers aren’t just salad dressing, but they actually shed light on memories and push the story further. Since Silent Hill uses the physical world to mirror a person’s mental state, it makes absolute sense that each character experiences reality a bit differently. The monstrosities that each sees are different as well, ranging from grotesque medical failures to others that represent corporate negligence. The one thing Townfall absolutely nails is the atmosphere. The retro-tech aesthetic of the late 1990s is so immersive and fits the theme so well, since this was the time period right before technology really boomed. There was email, but no world wide web, cell phones, tablets, billboards, or any of the things we see every day in the digital age now. Things were done manually and old school, with hand drawn signs and hand written notes. Townfall comes in at 51.18 gigs on the PlayStation 5, which is quite a size for a game that can be completed in only around 10-12 hours. Load times are decent, coming in at around 7 seconds to load in from the main menu. 3 difficulty options are offered: Story, Normal, and Nightmare, and Hinted and Normal are offered for puzzles. You also have settings to tweak show time played, adaptive triggers, auto aim, and letterbox aspect ratio. Not a bad suite of settings but you can’t rebind controls unfortunately. Technical performance is mostly solid, aside from a couple hard crashes that occurred during my playthrough and once when I got body blocked by an enemy that forced a reload. I encountered some frame dips too, even on Performance mode, though they didn’t really detract from the overall experience. Thankfully I’ve run into no bugs or other issues, and the ones I mentioned can easily be fixed with a Day One patch. Screen Burn proves once again what experts they are at masterful storytelling. Silent Hill: Townfall is another triumph in Motoi Okamoto’s revival of a new era for the franchise. This review is based on an early PS5 copy provided by the publisher. Silent Hill: Townfall comes out on September 24, 2026. Editor at GamingTrend who loves all things horror. But you'll see him playing all sorts of titles, because all games deserve a chance!

Ultimately, I found Townfall less impactful than Silent Hill 2 or Shattered Memories .
From the environments and puzzles, right down to the save system, which has always been a quirky thing in Silent Hill games.

Sneaking around the streets of St. Amelia. Its layout is ripe for creating your own paths to avoid enemies, and escaping their clutches by running down back alleys and hiding in cupboards is always a thrill. Plus, you get to explore a town that’s been lovingly and realistically rendered, with homes, shops, and features that offer a glimpse back to a simpler time. This man is Simon Ordell, wearing an outfit almost identical to Travis Grady’s from 2007’s Silent Hill: Origins , and denoting his everyman-ness. As you make your way up from the harbour, a cutscene plays, and a tarp blows away from a sign, revealing the town’s name: St. Amelia And so the game proper begins, as you make your way through the seemingly abandoned town to find out what’s going on. Along the way, you’ll take control of two additional characters besides Simon — Zoe and Richard — and the plot unfolds gradually to reveal the trio’s connection to one another. Complementing the visuals is the score, another feature that’s always stood out in Silent Hill titles. Here, though, regular series composer and sound designer Akira Yamaoka is, for once, not involved. Instead, the honors go to Pilotpriest, who’s done a fantastic job of replicating the off-kilter sounds and melancholic melodies fans have come to know and love, while adding a modern twist. Pieces are more sparse and muted than before, often with heavy doses of reverb. They match the tone of the gameplay brilliantly, and compositions open up during cutscenes when some emotional weight needs carrying. Another disappointing aspect of the game’s design is the monsters — this for a series renowned for its strikingly original creations. Virtually every one is some kind of faceless alabaster humanoid with no details of note, and some are mere rehashes of past favorites, such as the fleshy straight-jacketed figure, although this time it has a plank driven through its head. Less attention has been paid to their symbolism, too: there are suggestions that they reflect aspects of the inner turmoil of the main characters, à la most Silent Hill monsters, but there's little about their design that shows this in an interesting way. Zoe, on the other hand, is saddled with a pager, a far less effective item since it doesn’t directly reveal enemy movements. Instead, bars around the sides fill up to show their approximate direction and proximity. Both gadgets, though, are effective at grounding Townfall in the real world. At certain points, the CRTV can be tuned to show recorded messages that help develop the story or provide hints. The pager, meanwhile, receives mission- and story-related communication. This grounding is something the game as a whole does well. From the environments and puzzles, right down to the save system, which has always been a quirky thing in Silent Hill games. Usually, it’s something obscure and surreal, such as interacting with a well or a red square on a wall, but here you use landlines (no mobile phones in St. Amelia 1996) and dial 100 — the in-game number for the coastguard. The map screen is as helpful and skeuomorphic as ever. Scrawls in red marker pen appear to show rooms you’ve entered, locked doors, and story clues. You can also zoom and pan around it with ease. While I certainly had a good time with Townfall , certain sections drag on a little too long. But on the whole, the game does well to vary the environments and puzzles (the enemies less so) throughout to keep you hooked. I didn’t find normal difficulty too troubling: the puzzles are pitched just right, and those I spent a long time figuring out weren’t frustrating or unfair; in fact, they’re proved more satisfying to solve than the series’ typical offerings. It took me just over 20 hours to complete a single playthrough, and that was at a gentle pace. There’s little beyond the main objectives at hand to seek out, aside from some mysterious coded postcards that’ll have fans scrabbling to decipher, as well as hidden phone numbers to find. There are also unlockable outfits and weapons, and five different endings to get. Townfall isn’t particularly scary. There’s the occasional jump scare, but it doesn’t rely on them for cheap thrills. The game is a slow burn, with plenty of quiet, contemplative moments as you explore your surroundings. As with many Silent Hill games, the horror is more psychological. But herein lies a problem. While the story is commendable for sustaining the mystery for as long as possible, there’s a lack of character exploration, contrary to many other stories in the franchise. The characters’ dialogue is mostly cryptic, so you never get much of a grasp on their thoughts and feelings until the end — and even then, there are still plenty of questions left unanswered, as they should be. But the three of them are by turns confused and forlorn throughout. This mixture works to conjure that strange, uncanny tone the series is known for, but it also means the trio fails to elicit the same level of emotional investment garnered by past protagonists, such as Harry and Heather Mason, James Sunderland, and Mary. Social commentary seems to be Townfall’s primary concern: the main theme is one of corporate negligence and its devastating impact on a community, which is certainly relevant in today’s world. And it’s true that once the three collide and everything comes to a head, it starts to resonate emotionally. But this is a long time coming, and Zoe ultimately feels underserved by the story’s conclusion, a shame given the aforementioned excellence of her actor’s performance. It’s entirely possible, though, that other endings will give her a larger role than the one I reached, although I have no idea how these are achieved yet. Ultimately, I found Townfall less impactful than Silent Hill 2 or Shattered Memories . It won't haunt me for as long as those entries, but it’s an intriguing journey nonetheless, with mysteries that remain after completion to keep fans busy with their theories. No doubt some will also see Townfall as departing too far from the Silent Hill formula, a debate that’s already begun. But to my mind, the new setting and perspective fit the mold perfectly, so despite a few reservations, it still marks another triumphant reimagining of the series. You love sneaking and puzzling Sneaking around enemies is often thrilling, and the memorable puzzles mix realism with the series’ unhinged tropes masterfully. You want great art direction Screen Burn has managed to haul a small Scottish fishing village into the world of Silent Hill beautifully. It looks and sounds fantastic. You want the best monsters The monsters are certainly less memorable this time round, a shame given the series’ pedigree in this area. You want more emotion from your characters Mostly, the three protagonists are quite stilted in their tone. The botoxed facial animations don’t help, either. Compared to other modern releases, Townfall’s accessibility features are a little lacking. There are no content filters for blood and gore, and visual assists for color and contrast, and the like, are also missing. You can toggle subtitles and closed captions separately, though, and you can adjust the opacity of their backgrounds. There are three difficulty modes to choose from: Story, which reduces the threat posed by enemies; Normal, which is how the developers intend the game to be played; and Nightmare, which increases enemy power and makes your flashlight detectable by them. I played the game on a standard PS5, largely in Performance mode, although I also tested Quality mode for a time, too. I used a Lenovo Legion R27qe monitor and the Skullcandy Crusher PLYR 720 headset for audio.

It has classic psychological horror and grotesque monsters with the added benefit of the CRTV as a new puzzle solving and stealth tool. PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware. What is it? A single-player psychological horror game which takes place on an isolated Scottish island. The protagonist Simon Ordell has to solve puzzles, fight monsters, and figure out what the hell is going on. Release date September 24, 2026 Expect to pay $50 / £45 Developer Screen Burn Publisher Konami Reviewed on RTX 3070, Core AMD Ryzen 5 5600G, 16GB RAM Multiplayer No Steam Deck Unknown Link Steam Walking up to the old town of St Amelia for the first time in Silent Hill: Townfall, I was greeted by that familiar thick fog and eerie quiet—an omen of the horrors to come. I know what kind of monsters are waiting for me beyond the fog and I am painfully aware of just how unprepared I am for it—with no flashlight, healing items, or weapon on hand. But weirdly enough none of that matters, because for the first time in a Silent Hill game I feel content. St Amelia is a fictional town, but as I'm sure many players based in the UK will soon discover, developer Screen Burn breathes so much life into this sleepy fishing village that I could've sworn I'd been here before. It's certainly a strange feeling to have in a game like this, but with Konami opening Silent Hill up to the world it's now the UK's turn to have our sense of home toyed with. The story follows Simon Ordell, a man unknown to us and himself. The only sense of person he has comes from a medical bracelet with his name, date of birth, and blood type written on it. I watched as he dragged himself up from the waves of the North Sea, onto the docks, and headed into St Amelia seeking help and answers as to why he's here on this cold foggy island. A Silent Hill game is nothing without its setting and St Amelia delivers. I spent more time than I'd care to admit reading info boards about the history of fishing on the island and peeping over fences to see how the locals had done up their gardens. The more I explored, the better sense I got of the kind of people who lived in this town and what had happened to them. Simon also sees more than just the old town as he ventures to a hospital, a corporate office, your classic Silent Hill supernatural 'other place', and, brace yourself, some new builds. My time in St Amelia flew by rather quickly, with just 13 hours spent in total, but that was more than enough to be rewarded with heaps of brilliant visual storytelling and the usual gift of stressful encounters. St Amelia has its fair share of gut-wrenching horrors lurking around each corner, though—you don't spend a grand total of 35 minutes and five seconds hiding in lockers unless there's something pretty bad waiting for you on the other side. But even still, I found myself drawn to exploring the fog because my curiosity outweighed my fear. But the further I progressed the less content I became. Not because there were more faceless and bound monsters stumbling around (although that didn't help), but because there was more to the island than St Amelia's historic old town. There was a side that was painfully familiar—cobblestone streets shifted into tarmac roads and cottages were turned into flats for better efficiency. The island changed as Simon moved away from the heart of St Amelia and towards the parasite which had latched onto it. Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team. The town itself felt alive more than just lived in, and if that doesn't tick all the boxes for a world-class Silent Hill setting, I don't know what does. A good rule of thumb in Silent Hill is to approach its puzzles with lateral thinking, and Townfall is no different. They start fairly easy, coaching you in the art of taking in absolutely everything from your surroundings, digesting it, and then stitching together an answer from what has been gathered. It's the classic case of finding the combination to a lock by sifting through letters conveniently left scattered around the near vicinity. But as I spent more time in St Amelia, my brain gradually got the hang of looking at things from a Silent Hill perspective. And although the puzzles got harder it didn't feel like a noticeable difference. Hell, the first thing I thought when stumbling across a bunch of blood types scribbled across the wall was "This is a puzzle and it wants me to figure out how to create blood type A+". If it weren't for the 7+ hours I'd already spent in Townfall I doubt that would have been my default response. There were a few exceptions towards the very end of the game, however, I think a fresh brain would have had far less issues. Take the dreaded pipe room for example, where I had to use what looked to be morse code to twist a room full of levers in the right direction. After bashing my head against my desk my synapses sparked, a thought was formed, and I figured it out—I wish you all the best of luck with that one. The puzzles aren't the only smart design features in Townfall, though, with the best and brightest being the handheld CRTV. This quickly became my closest companion as it allowed me to see the creepies through any wall or obstacle. It may seem like a bit of a cheat code getting to know where the monsters are but there are some limitations. The CRTV may be the most creative, fun, and useful puzzle solving tool I've ever had the pleasure of playing with. I wouldn't say I'm much of a pacifist but I opted to forgo the planks of wood, pipes, and firearms for most of the game, instead favouring the CRTV as my weapon against the monsters to help me stealth around them. I played on the normal difficulty and I didn't have a run in with a monster until quite far into the latter stages of the game. They're not blind, I was just able to move around them with some ease if I used the CRTV correctly and was cautiously optimistic about how fast Simon could run. Even with all its finicky buttons the CRTV may be the most creative, fun, and useful puzzle solving tool I've ever had the pleasure of playing with. It turned navigating Townfall into one big scary puzzle, which is exactly what I look for in Silent Hill. But all of these amazing puzzles and fantastic world building would be for nought if Townfall hadn't also been able to pull off the kind of beautiful and psychologically jarring storytelling we've come to expect from the Silent Hill series. But the fact that there's something off about Simon isn't what interests me—the fun part is finding out what he did. To say there's something wrong with Simon would be to state the obvious. We're in a Silent Hill game after all, and no one in their sound mind would hallucinate grotesque faceless monsters which shoot needles out from their abdomens. But the fact that there's something off about Simon isn't what interests me—the fun part is finding out what he did to end up like this. It's clear that people in the town are angry, that some awful disaster happened on this island which rocked its community to its core. What's unclear, however, is why it involves some seemingly random American dude with induced amnesia. But Simon's not on his own. There are two other characters who also inhabit this liminal space with him—Zoe and Richard. At first I just thought these to be your typical filler characters but as it turns out these two are perhaps the most interesting characters to have ever fallen into the fog. My favourite sequence in all of Townfall was actually Zoe's part. In this she relives the aftermath of the disaster as a nurse and a first responder to the victims as she tries to save the life of an unknown patient. I am not a trained nurse so taking the patient's readings, running tests, and ultimately medicating them was probably one of the more stressful experiences I've had in a horror game. But it was worth it because through the stress I understood her guilt and trauma with painful clarity. It also made it clear why she's found herself wrapped up in this mess. Then there's Richard who is an opposite to Zoe in every sense of the word. He's not blameless or caring; he's an asshole. But boy, is he an interesting character study. I won't go into too much detail concerning Richard as his story is one that is better experienced firsthand. But, like with Zoe, after playing through his sequence it became clear to me what this game's curse is.
