What is it? A single-player psychological horror game which takes place on an isolated Scottish island. The protagonist Simon Ordell has to solve puzzles, fight monsters, and figure out what the hell is going on. Release date September 24, 2026 Expect to pay $50 / £45 Developer Screen Burn Publisher Konami Reviewed on RTX 3070, Core AMD Ryzen 5 5600G, 16GB RAM Multiplayer No Steam Deck Unknown Link Steam

Walking up to the old town of St Amelia for the first time in Silent Hill: Townfall, I was greeted by that familiar thick fog and eerie quiet—an omen of the horrors to come. I know what kind of monsters are waiting for me beyond the fog and I am painfully aware of just how unprepared I am for it—with no flashlight, healing items, or weapon on hand. But weirdly enough none of that matters, because for the first time in a Silent Hill game I feel content.

St Amelia is a fictional town, but as I'm sure many players based in the UK will soon discover, developer Screen Burn breathes so much life into this sleepy fishing village that I could've sworn I'd been here before. It's certainly a strange feeling to have in a game like this, but with Konami opening Silent Hill up to the world it's now the UK's turn to have our sense of home toyed with.

The story follows Simon Ordell, a man unknown to us and himself. The only sense of person he has comes from a medical bracelet with his name, date of birth, and blood type written on it. I watched as he dragged himself up from the waves of the North Sea, onto the docks, and headed into St Amelia seeking help and answers as to why he's here on this cold foggy island.

A Silent Hill game is nothing without its setting and St Amelia delivers. I spent more time than I'd care to admit reading info boards about the history of fishing on the island and peeping over fences to see how the locals had done up their gardens. The more I explored, the better sense I got of the kind of people who lived in this town and what had happened to them.

Simon also sees more than just the old town as he ventures to a hospital, a corporate office, your classic Silent Hill supernatural 'other place', and, brace yourself, some new builds. My time in St Amelia flew by rather quickly, with just 13 hours spent in total, but that was more than enough to be rewarded with heaps of brilliant visual storytelling and the usual gift of stressful encounters.

St Amelia has its fair share of gut-wrenching horrors lurking around each corner, though—you don't spend a grand total of 35 minutes and five seconds hiding in lockers unless there's something pretty bad waiting for you on the other side. But even still, I found myself drawn to exploring the fog because my curiosity outweighed my fear.

But the further I progressed the less content I became. Not because there were more faceless and bound monsters stumbling around (although that didn't help), but because there was more to the island than St Amelia's historic old town. There was a side that was painfully familiar—cobblestone streets shifted into tarmac roads and cottages were turned into flats for better efficiency. The island changed as Simon moved away from the heart of St Amelia and towards the parasite which had latched onto it.

The town itself felt alive more than just lived in, and if that doesn't tick all the boxes for a world-class Silent Hill setting, I don't know what does.

A good rule of thumb in Silent Hill is to approach its puzzles with lateral thinking, and Townfall is no different. They start fairly easy, coaching you in the art of taking in absolutely everything from your surroundings, digesting it, and then stitching together an answer from what has been gathered. It's the classic case of finding the combination to a lock by sifting through letters conveniently left scattered around the near vicinity.

But as I spent more time in St Amelia, my brain gradually got the hang of looking at things from a Silent Hill perspective. And although the puzzles got harder it didn't feel like a noticeable difference. Hell, the first thing I thought when stumbling across a bunch of blood types scribbled across the wall was "This is a puzzle and it wants me to figure out how to create blood type A+". If it weren't for the 7+ hours I'd already spent in Townfall I doubt that would have been my default response.

There were a few exceptions towards the very end of the game, however, I think a fresh brain would have had far less issues. Take the dreaded pipe room for example, where I had to use what looked to be morse code to twist a room full of levers in the right direction. After bashing my head against my desk my synapses sparked, a thought was formed, and I figured it out—I wish you all the best of luck with that one.

The puzzles aren't the only smart design features in Townfall, though, with the best and brightest being the handheld CRTV. This quickly became my closest companion as it allowed me to see the creepies through any wall or obstacle. It may seem like a bit of a cheat code getting to know where the monsters are but there are some limitations.
The CRTV may be the most creative, fun, and useful puzzle solving tool I've ever had the pleasure of playing with.

I wouldn't say I'm much of a pacifist but I opted to forgo the planks of wood, pipes, and firearms for most of the game, instead favouring the CRTV as my weapon against the monsters to help me stealth around them. I played on the normal difficulty and I didn't have a run in with a monster until quite far into the latter stages of the game. They're not blind, I was just able to move around them with some ease if I used the CRTV correctly and was cautiously optimistic about how fast Simon could run.

Even with all its finicky buttons the CRTV may be the most creative, fun, and useful puzzle solving tool I've ever had the pleasure of playing with. It turned navigating Townfall into one big scary puzzle, which is exactly what I look for in Silent Hill.

But all of these amazing puzzles and fantastic world building would be for nought if Townfall hadn't also been able to pull off the kind of beautiful and psychologically jarring storytelling we've come to expect from the Silent Hill series.
But the fact that there's something off about Simon isn't what interests me—the fun part is finding out what he did.

To say there's something wrong with Simon would be to state the obvious. We're in a Silent Hill game after all, and no one in their sound mind would hallucinate grotesque faceless monsters which shoot needles out from their abdomens. But the fact that there's something off about Simon isn't what interests me—the fun part is finding out what he did to end up like this. It's clear that people in the town are angry, that some awful disaster happened on this island which rocked its community to its core. What's unclear, however, is why it involves some seemingly random American dude with induced amnesia.

But Simon's not on his own. There are two other characters who also inhabit this liminal space with him—Zoe and Richard. At first I just thought these to be your typical filler characters but as it turns out these two are perhaps the most interesting characters to have ever fallen into the fog.

My favourite sequence in all of Townfall was actually Zoe's part. In this she relives the aftermath of the disaster as a nurse and a first responder to the victims as she tries to save the life of an unknown patient.

I am not a trained nurse so taking the patient's readings, running tests, and ultimately medicating them was probably one of the more stressful experiences I've had in a horror game. But it was worth it because through the stress I understood her guilt and trauma with painful clarity. It also made it clear why she's found herself wrapped up in this mess.

Then there's Richard who is an opposite to Zoe in every sense of the word. He's not blameless or caring; he's an asshole. But boy, is he an interesting character study. I won't go into too much detail concerning Richard as his story is one that is better experienced firsthand. But, like with Zoe, after playing through his sequence it became clear to me what this game's curse is. While the answer seemed simple at first examining the curse through the lens of three different characters adds enough diversity for an incredibly rewarding story and analysis of its characters.

My only issue with Townfall was that I didn't get to spend more time with Zoe and Richard, because in comparison Simon is just a little boring. His role as a blank template for players to print themselves onto worked wonders for immersion but ultimately his character suffered for it. I found myself drawn more to Zoe and Richard, two characters who had more invested in this community from the get go.

That's not to say I dislike Simon. He's a fantastic character who comes into his own during the latter stages of the story and is someone who will grow on me the more time I spend mulling Townfall over.

After all was said and done and I'd finally reached the end of Townfall's brilliant story, my overwhelming feeling was one of relief. Like Silent Hill f before it, Townfall had some monumental expectations to live up to and the unenviable task of proving that yet again the mystique of Silent Hill is not limited to one mountainous town. But it's now clear that Screen Burn absolutely understands what makes a great Silent Hill game and the series is better off for it.

extraction.body: The Silent Hill franchise is having a resurgence, and I’m all for it. With 3 straight autumns of new releases: Silent Hill 2 Remake, Silent Hill f, and now Silent Hill: Townfall, fans are in for a treat with this new rendition. After playing through all 3, I’m genuinely impressed with how much each individual title stands out from one another. Screen Burn has done an incredible job crafting their own version of Silent Hill, and Townfall might be the best one yet. I was initially worried after my hands-on preview that Townfall might be a rehash of Silent Hill 2, but boy was I wrong. Screen Burn wasn’t lying when they said the game would be social commentary around big corporations, coverups, and whistleblowers. The narrative truly does deliver here, and with several endings to achieve, I’ll have to see them all to get the full picture of the story and message. Pacing is also excellent, with the overall length of the gaming feeling just right, not too short, and not too long. If you want a brief refresher on what the game is, check out my preview. You do get to step into the perspective of other characters, Zoe and Richard. All of them have ties to one another in some way. Not only does this allow you to see a different side of the narrative, piecing together things that were confusing to you before, but it also forces you to play a bit differently than Simon. Zoe starts off with absolutely nothing other than a pager, meaning she doesn’t have the CRTV to help locate threats or a melee weapon to defend herself. You have to rely on pure stealth to pass her sections. Richard, on the other hand, starts off with a shotgun, and the game absolutely showers you with ammo, so feel free to go to town with anything that comes your way. The “survival horror” gameplay might not break the typical mold of the genre, but Townfall does so with confidence and grace. Why fix what ain’t broke right? Ammunition is scarce, melee weapons like wooden sticks and pipes degrade and break, and healing items can be crafted to create better ones. The only real new additions are Simon’s CRTV and his IV bag that acts as a second life if he is fatally struck. You’ll be switching between pure stealth sections and hybrid stealth and combat portions, and the cadence and transitions help it not to feel forced or weird. The Alien Isolation influence is seen clearly, with several spaces to hide in, radios to turn on to draw attention, and bottles and bricks to throw to distract. Gunplay, on the other hand, is crisp and responsive, and for the revolver, you can physically see yourself reloading all 6 bullets into the chamber before you can fire again. Simon gets his hands on a flare gun later in the game too. The gameplay and narrative sail smoothly into one another in a way that feels like natural progression. My only complaint is that some forced stealth sections are a bit too dragged out. In the middle chapter of the game, there is a Mr. X-like entity that is unkillable and will one-shot you if you’re caught. These sections last a bit too long for my liking. The enemy AI is a tad too sensitive, so any small movement will trigger them, forcing you to hide and de-aggro them. Normally immense backtracking would be a point of contention with horror titles, but Townfall strikes a good balance at this. You’re never really treading the same path more than a couple times, and levels are intricately designed so that you might find a new path to a previously visited area. This is also true when you play as different characters, so don’t worry about them tasking you to do the same thing twice. This is not a game that holds your hand, even on “Hinted” difficulty for puzzles. You’ll have to think outside the box or even brute force some solutions if you can’t figure them out. That being said, I absolutely adored the variety of riddles that range from your typical image alignment with the CRTV all the way to more complex ones that require you to keep track of several key factors and backtrack to previously inaccessible areas. My favorite involved finding blood bags of different patients and piecing together their blood types. There were ones that veered on the edge of being too obscure, so take that as you will. Like I mentioned in my preview, these brainteasers aren’t just salad dressing, but they actually shed light on memories and push the story further. Since Silent Hill uses the physical world to mirror a person’s mental state, it makes absolute sense that each character experiences reality a bit differently. The monstrosities that each sees are different as well, ranging from grotesque medical failures to others that represent corporate negligence. The one thing Townfall absolutely nails is the atmosphere. The retro-tech aesthetic of the late 1990s is so immersive and fits the theme so well, since this was the time period right before technology really boomed. There was email, but no world wide web, cell phones, tablets, billboards, or any of the things we see every day in the digital age now. Things were done manually and old school, with hand drawn signs and hand written notes. Townfall comes in at 51.18 gigs on the PlayStation 5, which is quite a size for a game that can be completed in only around 10-12 hours. Load times are decent, coming in at around 7 seconds to load in from the main menu. 3 difficulty options are offered: Story, Normal, and Nightmare, and Hinted and Normal are offered for puzzles. You also have settings to tweak show time played, adaptive triggers, auto aim, and letterbox aspect ratio. Not a bad suite of settings but you can’t rebind controls unfortunately. Technical performance is mostly solid, aside from a couple hard crashes that occurred during my playthrough and once when I got body blocked by an enemy that forced a reload. I encountered some frame dips too, even on Performance mode, though they didn’t really detract from the overall experience. Thankfully I’ve run into no bugs or other issues, and the ones I mentioned can easily be fixed with a Day One patch. Screen Burn proves once again what experts they are at masterful storytelling. Silent Hill: Townfall is another triumph in Motoi Okamoto’s revival of a new era for the franchise. This review is based on an early PS5 copy provided by the publisher. Silent Hill: Townfall comes out on September 24, 2026. Editor at GamingTrend who loves all things horror. But you'll see him playing all sorts of titles, because all games deserve a chance!

extraction.body: President presses case for controversial $400m project following White House correspondents’ dinner shooting President presses case for controversial $400m project following White House correspondents’ dinner shooting The shooting at the Washington Hilton hotel gives new urgency to the project to construct a 1,000-seat ballroom at the White House, Donald Trump claimed after the incident on Saturday night. The US president pressed the case for his controversial ballroom initiative at the press conference he held at the White House on Saturday and a social media post on Sunday, after an armed attacker was arrested as he rushed towards the Hilton’s ballroom, where Trump was attending the White House Correspondents Association’s annual dinner . The $400m construction project to build a giant event space began at the White House with the East Wing being knocked down last October without Trump waiting for full legal permission to proceed. Legal challenges followed along with controversy over funding for the enormous ballroom, which is planned to be larger than the core White House itself. “What happened last night is exactly the reason that our great Military, Secret Service, Law Enforcement and, for different reasons, every President for the last 150 years, have been DEMANDING that a large, safe, and secure Ballroom be built ON THE GROUNDS OF THE WHITE HOUSE,” Trump posted on Truth Social on Sunday morning. He said that the shooting incident, which caused Trump and senior administration to be hustled out of the Hilton hotel complex, and hundreds of guests to duck for cover, “would never have happened with the Militarily Top Secret Ballroom currently under construction at the White House”. Trump pointed to existing security at the White House – “the most secure building in the world” – and “every highest level security feature there is” planned for the ballroom. “Plus, there are no rooms sitting on top for unsecured people to pour in,” he added, referring to the event taking place in a mainstream hotel. Trump’s comments were the second time in just over 12 hours that he mentioned the White House ballroom project in reference to the shooting incident. “I didn’t want to say this,” Trump said at a press briefing late Saturday after returning to the White House from the press dinner, “but this is why we have to have all of the attributes of what we’re planning at the White House. It’s actually a larger room, and it’s a much more secure. It’s got – it’s drone-proof, it’s bulletproof glass.” Trump has survived two previous assassination attempts, both during his 2024 election campaign. After the latest incident, Trump said in the White House briefing room that the scare would not affect the conduct of his life. “I like not to think about it,” he said. “I lead a pretty normal life, considering, you know, it’s a dangerous life. I think I’m, I think I handle it as well – as well as it can be handled. “To be honest with you, I’m not a basket case,” he added. But he also conceded that “it’s always shocking when something like this happens” and it had been “very unexpected”. He told Weijia Jiang, the CBS News correspondent and the president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, who was seated to his left at the dinner, that she had done “a fantastic job. What a beautiful evening.” Trump said he thought the noise that later turned out to be gunfire was “a tray going down. I’ve heard that many times, and it was a pretty loud noise, and it was from quite far away.” Melania Trump, he said, “was very cognizant, I think, of what happened. I think she knew immediately what happened. She was saying: ‘That’s a bad noise.’” Trump said it was “a rather traumatic experience for her”. Trump had been expected to roast the attending press corps during an after-dinner speech with what he said would have been the “most inappropriate speech ever made”. Even his being invited to the dinner was controversial after several years of calling the US media “the enemy of the people”. The $400m construction project to build a giant event space began at the White House with the East Wing being knocked down last October without Trump waiting for full legal permission to proceed. extraction.body: WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal appeals court on Friday ordered President Donald Trump's administration to halt construction of its $400 million ballroom at the White House because the project lacks congressional approval. Trump doesn't have the unilateral authority to build a 90,000-square-foot (8,400-square-meter) ballroom where the White House's East Wing stood before he ordered its demolition last fall, according to the decision by a three-judge panel from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. The Republican president said in a post on social media that he would be appealing what he called an "unjust decision" to the U.S. Supreme Court. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Friday's ruling marked the second time this week the Trump administration has made headlines for construction plans that have been called into question. An assessment by the National Park Service found that a 250-foot-tall (76-meter-tall) triumphal arch that Trump has proposed building could compromise the historical significance of dozens of sites near its planned location on a traffic circle between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. In a 2-1 decision on the ballroom, the appeals court sided with historic preservationists who sued to stop construction of the massive structure, which has begun to rise aboveground on the east side of the White House, according to the most recent aerial photos of the site. The court said it would stay its ruling for two weeks to give the administration time to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court. "Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help," the court wrote. "This holding has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable, or not, as a matter of policy. This ruling does not even necessarily mean that the Defendants may not ultimately construct the ballroom. "What it does mean," the court continued, "is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court's expeditious litigation without securing Congress's authorization, as the Constitution and laws require." The president reacted to the ruling with a lengthy post on social media in which he quoted from a dissenting opinion issued by Judge Neomi Rao, whom he nominated. He also described the plans for the facility to include bomb shelters, a hospital and medical facilities, "Top Secret Military Facilities" and other security features. "The Military and Secret Service are viewing this horrendous, politically motivated, and unlawful ruling as a National Security threat to our Nation in that the entire Complex is being built for the protection of our Country and, additionally, all future Presidents," Trump wrote. After the lower court earlier this year ordered a halt to aboveground construction, the president argued that permission from Congress to build the ballroom was unnecessary because public money was not being used to pay for it. Trump has said he has raised hundreds of millions of dollars from corporations and wealthy people, including himself, to cover the construction costs. But the Trump administration requested $1 billion for the ballroom, which Congress refused in May. In June, Democrats warned that $350 million in funds from a tax cuts law appeared to have been redirected for the ballroom. WATCH: Trump calls planned White House ballroom 'a gift' to U.S. The National Trust for Historic Preservation, the nonprofit organization that brought the lawsuit against the Trump administration, said Friday's decision affirmed "the American people's right to voice their opinions about the historic places they cherish," including the White House. "From the beginning, our position has been clear and consistent: the law states that only Congress can authorize the construction of a ballroom at the White House," Brent Leggs, the group's president and CEO, said in a statement. "We are pleased with the DC Circuit Court's decision to uphold the District Court's preliminary injunction, which although stayed for 14 days will block any above-ground ballroom construction unless and until Congress takes action." The divided appeals court panel upheld an April 16 order from Leon for the Trump administration to halt aboveground work on the ballroom. Leon, who was nominated to the bench by Republican President George W. Bush, allowed construction to continue on underground work on a bunker and other "national security facilities" at the site. The appeals court case was assigned to Judges Rao, Patricia Millett and Bradley Garcia. Millett was nominated to the court by Democratic President Barack Obama. Garcia was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden. Both Millett and Garcia backed the decision, while Rao opposed it. The National Trust for Historic Preservation sued to challenge the project in December 2025, a week after completion of the East Wing demolition to make way for a ballroom that Trump says would hold 999 people. Government lawyers have argued that the project — the biggest structural change to the White House in more than 70 years — must move forward because it includes critical security features to guard against a range of threats, such as drones, ballistic missiles and biohazards. "These upgrades, alterations, and improvements are essential to protecting the President, his family, and his staff, as well as the White House itself, and the entire project flows from them," government attorneys wrote in a court filing. Attorneys for the preservation group countered that the lack of a White House ballroom doesn't constitute a national security emergency. "That commonsense conclusion is not clearly erroneous, and there is no basis to disturb it," they wrote. In an initial ruling that the government also appealed, Leon barred aboveground work on the ballroom from proceeding without congressional approval. In response, the appeals court instructed the judge to reconsider the national security implications of stopping construction. In his most recent decision, Leon ordered a stop only to the aboveground construction of the planned ballroom. The judge stressed that the White House is free to proceed with underground work, including the construction of any bunkers, military installations and medical facilities. On April 2, Trump's ballroom won final approval from the 12-member National Capital Planning Commission, which is charged with approving construction on federal property in the Washington region. Associated Press writers Bill Barrow in Atlanta and Gary Fields and Michelle L. Price in Washington contributed to this report. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. extraction.body: President presses case for controversial $400m project following White House correspondents’ dinner shooting President presses case for controversial $400m project following White House correspondents’ dinner shooting The shooting at the Washington Hilton hotel gives new urgency to the project to construct a 1,000-seat ballroom at the White House, Donald Trump claimed after the incident on Saturday night. The US president pressed the case for his controversial ballroom initiative at the press conference he held at the White House on Saturday and a social media post on Sunday, after an armed attacker was arrested as he rushed towards the Hilton’s ballroom, where Trump was attending the White House Correspondents Association’s annual dinner . The $400m construction project to build a giant event space began at the White House with the East Wing being knocked down last October without Trump waiting for full legal permission to proceed. Legal challenges followed along with controversy over funding for the enormous ballroom, which is planned to be larger than the core White House itself. “What happened last night is exactly the reason that our great Military, Secret Service, Law Enforcement and, for different reasons, every President for the last 150 years, have been DEMANDING that a large, safe, and secure Ballroom be built ON THE GROUNDS OF THE WHITE HOUSE,” Trump posted on Truth Social on Sunday morning. He said that the shooting incident, which caused Trump and senior administration to be hustled out of the Hilton hotel complex, and hundreds of guests to duck for cover, “would never have happened with the Militarily Top Secret Ballroom currently under construction at the White House”. Trump pointed to existing security at the White House – “the most secure building in the world” – and “every highest level security feature there is” planned for the ballroom. “Plus, there are no rooms sitting on top for unsecured people to pour in,” he added, referring to the event taking place in a mainstream hotel. Trump’s comments were the second time in just over 12 hours that he mentioned the White House ballroom project in reference to the shooting incident. “I didn’t want to say this,” Trump said at a press briefing late Saturday after returning to the White House from the press dinner, “but this is why we have to have all of the attributes of what we’re planning at the White House. It’s actually a larger room, and it’s a much more secure. It’s got – it’s drone-proof, it’s bulletproof glass.” Trump has survived two previous assassination attempts, both during his 2024 election campaign. After the latest incident, Trump said in the White House briefing room that the scare would not affect the conduct of his life. “I like not to think about it,” he said. “I lead a pretty normal life, considering, you know, it’s a dangerous life. I think I’m, I think I handle it as well – as well as it can be handled. “To be honest with you, I’m not a basket case,” he added. But he also conceded that “it’s always shocking when something like this happens” and it had been “very unexpected”. He told Weijia Jiang, the CBS News correspondent and the president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, who was seated to his left at the dinner, that she had done “a fantastic job. What a beautiful evening.” Trump said he thought the noise that later turned out to be gunfire was “a tray going down. I’ve heard that many times, and it was a pretty loud noise, and it was from quite far away.” Melania Trump, he said, “was very cognizant, I think, of what happened. I think she knew immediately what happened. She was saying: ‘That’s a bad noise.’” Trump said it was “a rather traumatic experience for her”. Trump had been expected to roast the attending press corps during an after-dinner speech with what he said would have been the “most inappropriate speech ever made”. Even his being invited to the dinner was controversial after several years of calling the US media “the enemy of the people”. He has been repeatedly suing various media outlets, threatening broadcasters over their licenses and stepping up his attacks on some individual journalists when they ask him awkward questions. On Saturday night he suddenly now thanked the gathered journalists at the White House press briefing room, most still in the eveningwear they had donned for the dinner event. He praised “very responsible” coverage of the drama that had unfolded and said that when the press dinner is reorganized he is likely to give a different speech than the one he had planned for Saturday night. Then on Sunday, Trump said lawsuits seeking to stop the White House ballroom construction “must be dropped, immediately”, adding: “Nothing should be allowed to interfere with with its construction, which is on budget and substantially ahead of schedule.” That view was supported by at least one moderate Democrat, Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman. “That venue wasn’t built to accommodate an event with the line of succession for the US government,” Fetterman posted on X , referring to the Washington Hilton. “After witnessing last night, drop the TDS (‘Trump Derangement Syndrome’), and build the White House ballroom for events exactly like these,” he said.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump on Sunday assailed a federal judge’s injunction halting aboveground construction of the White House ballroom, emphasizing the enhanced security features that form a key part of the project. In a post on Truth Social, the president wrote that U.S. District Judge Richard Leon, a George W. Bush appointee, should “stop playing games with America’s Security.” Trump added an ominous warning that if anything were to happen, the judge “will be responsible for the Death and Destruction caused to our Country.” “He has already created enough problems by allowing ‘Top Secret’ information to be released and exposed based on a ridiculous lawsuit started by a highly litigious woman,” Trump noted. The National Trust for Historic Preservation filed a lawsuit in December to block the $400 million project, arguing that it cannot proceed until it receives congressional authorization. Leon agreed at the end of March, but that decision was later paused by a federal appeals court, allowing work to resume in the interim pending further review. The president invoked national security as a justification for forging ahead. His Sunday post featured two AI-generated renderings of military-style drones stationed on the rooftop and flanked by snipers. “The DronePort at the White House Ballroom will be, perhaps, the most sophisticated anywhere in the World! It will safeguard our Nation’s Capital, Washington, D.C., long into the future,” Trump said. “With the advent of highly sophisticated, and powerful, modern day weaponry, we can no longer defend Washington, D.C., with rifles and pistols, alone.” Trump hosted reporters for a tour of the site of the former East Wing in May, where he cast the development as both a ballroom and a fortress. Among the features he highlighted were a military hospital, missile-proof roofing and a “drone port” designed to accommodate an “unlimited number of drones.” “This is all my money and donors’ money. This is tax free,” Trump asserted. “On top of the roof, we’re going to have the greatest drone empire that you’ve ever seen and it’s going to protect Washington.” It remains unclear how or why drones would be deployed in this way. The specifics of security at the White House are not widely discussed but it has been reported that the building already has measures in place to combat potential drone attacks. Security in general is a significant concern, however. Over the past month, there have been three separate incidents in which gunfire erupted in close proximity to the president. On May 23, a gunman approached the White House while Trump was inside the residence, drew a firearm and discharged multiple rounds before being fatally shot by Secret Service agents. On May 4, a man was wounded during a firefight with Secret Service personnel near the Washington Monument. On April 25, an individual carrying a shotgun, handgun and knives attempted to breach a security checkpoint at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner — an event attended by the president — before being swiftly apprehended by law enforcement and charged with attempting to assassinate the president. The Justice Department is hoping the security imperatives will shape the trajectory of the legal dispute. An assessment by the National Park Service found that a 250-foot-tall (76-meter-tall) triumphal arch that Trump has proposed building could compromise the historical significance of dozens of sites near its planned location on a traffic circle between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. The court said it would stay its ruling for two weeks to give the administration time to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court. "Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help," the court wrote. This ruling does not even necessarily mean that the Defendants may not ultimately construct the ballroom. "What it does mean," the court continued, "is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court's expeditious litigation without securing Congress's authorization, as the Constitution and laws require." The president reacted to the ruling with a lengthy post on social media in which he quoted from a dissenting opinion issued by Judge Neomi Rao, whom he nominated. He also described the plans for the facility to include bomb shelters, a hospital and medical facilities, "Top Secret Military Facilities" and other security features. Trump has said he has raised hundreds of millions of dollars from corporations and wealthy people, including himself, to cover the construction costs. But the Trump administration requested $1 billion for the ballroom, which Congress refused in May. In June, Democrats warned that $350 million in funds from a tax cuts law appeared to have been redirected for the ballroom. "From the beginning, our position has been clear and consistent: the law states that only Congress can authorize the construction of a ballroom at the White House," Brent Leggs, the group's president and CEO, said in a statement. "We are pleased with the DC Circuit Court's decision to uphold the District Court's preliminary injunction, which although stayed for 14 days will block any above-ground ballroom construction unless and until Congress takes action." "That commonsense conclusion is not clearly erroneous, and there is no basis to disturb it," they wrote. In an initial ruling that the government also appealed, Leon barred aboveground work on the ballroom from proceeding without congressional approval. In response, the appeals court instructed the judge to reconsider the national security implications of stopping construction. In his most recent decision, Leon ordered a stop only to the aboveground construction of the planned ballroom. The judge stressed that the White House is free to proceed with underground work, including the construction of any bunkers, military installations and medical facilities. extraction.body: The shooting outside the White House Correspondents’ Dinner on Saturday evening has thrust fresh attention on President Donald Trump’s push to build a secure ballroom at the White House, a proposal he says could prevent such threats. A gunman armed with multiple weapons opened fire near a security checkpoint at the Washington Hilton — where hundreds of journalists, celebrities and government officials were attending the annual White House Correspondents’ Dinner. A Secret Service agent was struck but protected by a ballistic vest, and the suspect was quickly taken into custody, authorities said. Trump told reporters at the White House that he spoke with the agent, adding that he is expected to recover. SECRET SERVICE IN LINE OF FIRE AT WHCD SHOOTING STILL UNPAID DUE TO DEM-LED SHUTDOWN Trump pointed to the incident as evidence that the hotel venue was "not a particularly secure building," arguing that a new White House ballroom — equipped with features like bulletproof materials — would offer a safer alternative. While the White House has hosted countless ceremonial events, it has never had a dedicated ballroom. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the ballroom would seat roughly 650 guests and reflect the building’s classical design. "The White House is currently unable to host major functions honoring world leaders… without having to install a large and unsightly tent approximately 100 yards away," Leavitt said during a July 31 briefing, calling the project "a much-needed and exquisite addition." FROM THE OVAL OFFICE TO THE TRUMP KENNEDY CENTER, THE GILDED MAKEOVER EXPANDS Since returning to office, Trump, a former real estate developer, has embarked on a series of projects aimed at altering the look and feel of the White House and other iconic Washington landmarks. In February, the president announced in a Truth Social post that the Trump Kennedy Center will close for a two-year renovation. The monument, a near twin of Paris’ iconic Arc de Triomphe, is meant to welcome visitors crossing the Memorial Bridge from Arlington National Cemetery into the heart of the nation’s capital. Trump has also added golden accents to the Oval Office, added a "walk of fame" to the colonnade outside the Oval Office, renovated the Lincoln bathroom, paved part of the Rose Garden and installed two large American flags on the White House grounds.

Government has to be regulating this.” Venture capitalist David Sacks served as Trump’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March, when he stepped down after reaching his time limit as a special government employee. A White House official also said that AI safety would be “on the agenda” when Trump meets with Xi.

extraction.body: US President Donald Trump has announced that he will form an "AI Force" and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar amid warnings about the emergent technology. In a social media post on Saturday, he said his administration "will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth" of the industry, and pushed back against calls to slow down the development of AI until better safeguards are put in place. His post came as a slew of warnings about the potential dangers of AI have spurred calls for coordinated action on the technology's development. Trump offered no details or a timeline for his plan. Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings "AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country's GDP," he said on social media, adding that he wants the US to continue leading China in AI. AI now sits at the heart of the US-China rivalry as the world's two largest economies seek to gain an edge in advanced tech, and it is expected to be discussed when Trump meets President Xi Jinping next week. Meanwhile, Trump said his administration would use the existing criminal and civil justice system to target any bad actors using the AI. He also repeated comments that criticism and concerns around the potential dangers of AI are a "hoax". Watch: Cyber Correspondent Joe Tidy considers if could AI wipe out humanity, and how it might do it Claims by current and former researchers that the tech will endanger humanity - with one suggesting there is a greater than 10% chance of it "killing all humans" - have raised alarm bells in recent weeks. Major AI companies have been racing to develop better systems, including creating what they call super intelligence - theoretical tech which is smarter than humans. AI titans Anthropic, OpenAI and Google - the tech companies behind Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, respectively - have also disclosed instances of security breaches or incidents in which their chatbots were used for "malicious activity". Anthropic head Dario Amodei recently called for AI development to slow down and proposed industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development. Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of xAI have both said they agree with his recommendations. Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic, told BBC that a "kill switch" that can be checked by a third party may need to be mandatory for the industry. The warnings have prompted US lawmakers to propose legislation around the technology but Altman suggested this week that Washington has struggled to keep pace with the new tech and how to regulate it. He said people should have more faith in AI firms to keep it safe. "The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Altman told a conference in San Francisco. In the UK, MPs across parties and peers have identified human rights risks posed by artificial intelligence and have argued that existing laws are ill-equipped to address the technology's rapid growth. The Joint Committee on Human Rights (JCHR) has published a report calling for a new bill on AI to "address the scale and seriousness" of such threats. extraction.body: Shares of U.S.-listed companies exposed to Greenland surged on Monday after the U.S. and Denmark reached a deal on security arrangements on the Arctic territory. Shares of Greenland Energy soared more than 165% during premarket trading, with Greenland Mines seen up over 110% and Critical Metals Corp nearly 26% higher. The agreement, which is expected to be signed during the United Nations General Assembly this week, will see the U.S., Denmark and Greenland enter into a pact to develop a significant military presence on the territory, while blocking Washington's adversaries from building their own bases there. It follows several months of U.S. President Donald Trum p's threats to annex the self-governing Danish territory, with the president insisting Greenland is critical to U.S. national security. Announcing the deal, Trump said via Truth Social on Friday that the U.S. would "FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America." Trump said the agreement would come at no cost to the U.S., adding that Washington would "immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many." Key details of the agreement have not yet been made public. Greenlandic and Danish officials sought to reassure citizens over the weekend that the deal would respect the island's right to self-determination and the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom. "It is joyous that we are about to make an agreement that will ensure and strengthen the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western Alliance," Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said in a statement. "The agreement recognizes Greenland's interests and our place in the international cooperation. It is to the benefit of us all," he added. Greenland Energy is an oil and gas exploration firm focused on trying to unlock the hydrocarbon potential of the Jameson Land Basin on the island's east coast. The Texas-based company, which has links to Trump , recently delayed plans to drill for oil in Greenland after the island's government issued a " strong warning " to its joint venture partner for bringing equipment ashore without permission. Greenland Mines, meanwhile, is a natural resources company working on the Skaergaard Project, which ranks among the world's largest undeveloped palladium, gold and platinum deposits. Critical Metals Corp, for its part, is a mining company focused on critical metals and minerals and is developing the Tanbreez rare earths mine in southern Greenland. Got a confidential news tip? The rally followed a U.S.-Denmark-Greenland security pact aimed at expanding the military presence on the Arctic territory. Stocks of U.S.-listed companies with operational ties to Greenland experienced significant gains on Monday following the announcement of a new security agreement between the United States, Denmark, and Greenland. The trilateral pact, announced by U.S. President Donald Trump, aims to substantially expand the American military presence in the strategically vital Arctic territory. The market reaction was immediate and forceful across the basic materials sector. Shares of Greenland Energy (GLND) jumped 119 percent in extended trading, while Greenland Mines (GGRML) rose 58 percent. Critical Metals Corp (CRML) also saw a 20 percent increase. The surge reflects intense investor anticipation that the military agreement will pave the way for increased U.S. infrastructure investment and financial support for resource extraction in the region. While the diplomatic arrangement focuses explicitly on defense and preventing geopolitical adversaries from establishing Arctic bases, private capital is aggressively pricing in the secondary economic benefits of a reinforced American security umbrella. The pact is expected to be formally signed later this week during the United Nations General Assembly in New York. The new security arrangement places Arctic access at the center of U.S. foreign policy. Historically, the United States has maintained a critical strategic foothold in Greenland through the Thule Air Base—recently renamed Pituffik Space Base—which operates early warning radar systems essential for North American aerospace defense. The new pact is designed to expand this presence, allowing for greater troop deployments, maritime coordination, and shared intelligence operations. For the defense infrastructure to function effectively in the harsh Arctic environment, significant logistical upgrades are required. Military expansion inherently demands improved deep-water ports, reinforced airstrips, and robust telecommunications networks. It is this anticipated dual-use infrastructure that has galvanized the equity markets, as mining and energy companies operating in Greenland frequently cite severe logistical bottlenecks as their primary operational constraint. The agreement emerges against a backdrop of escalating geopolitical competition. As the polar ice caps retreat, new shipping routes are opening, and the race to secure access to the Arctic seabed has intensified. Both Russia and China have expressed strong strategic interest in the region, prompting Washington to solidify its alliances with Copenhagen and the semi-autonomous government in Nuuk. The dramatic rise in Greenland-linked equities highlights the speculative nature of frontier market investing. The current surge draws direct comparisons to August 2019 and earlier in 2026, when President Trump publicly floated the idea of the United States purchasing Greenland outright. While those proposals were swiftly rejected by Danish and Greenlandic officials, they successfully signaled to the market that Washington views the island as a paramount national security interest. However, analysts caution that the current rally is built heavily on projection rather than immediate commercial reality. The security pact announced on Monday did not include specific commercial funding, fast-tracked mining permits, or direct subsidies for the resource sector. Companies like Greenland Mines and Critical Metals remain in the exploratory or early developmental stages, facing immense environmental and regulatory hurdles before they can achieve commercial production. The primary economic draw of Greenland lies in its vast, largely untapped deposits of rare earth elements, uranium, and base metals. These materials are critical for the global energy transition, powering everything from electric vehicle batteries to advanced military guidance systems. Currently, global supply chains for rare earth elements are heavily dominated by China, creating an urgent accountability mandate for Western governments to secure independent supply lines. By expanding its military footprint, the U.S. government is effectively de-risking the jurisdiction for private capital. However, the ultimate authority over resource extraction resides with the Greenlandic government in Nuuk. Local authorities must balance the promise of economic independence—fueled by mining royalties—with profound environmental concerns and the preservation of traditional Indigenous ways of life. The intersection of military expansion and speculative mining carries profound implications for Greenland's population of roughly 56,000 people. While the influx of American capital could provide the economic foundation necessary for Greenland to pursue full independence from Denmark, it also risks overwhelming local institutions. The rapid industrialization of pristine Arctic environments remains a highly contentious domestic political issue. For the companies whose stocks surged this week, the challenge will be translating geopolitical momentum into operational success. The harsh climate, lack of existing infrastructure, and stringent environmental regulations mean that establishing a profitable mine in Greenland requires billions of dollars in upfront capital and years of patient development. Investors and policy analysts are now looking toward the United Nations General Assembly, where the formal signing of the pact is expected to yield specific details regarding troop deployments and infrastructure commitments. The ultimate test of Monday's market rally will be whether the U.S. government follows its military agreements with concrete financial mechanisms, such as Export-Import Bank financing, to support the commercial ambitions of the surging equities. The new pact is designed to expand this presence, allowing for greater troop deployments, maritime coordination, and shared intelligence operations.

For the defense infrastructure to function effectively in the harsh Arctic environment, significant logistical upgrades are required. Military expansion inherently demands improved deep-water ports, reinforced airstrips, and robust telecommunications networks. It is this anticipated dual-use infrastructure that has galvanized the equity markets, as mining and energy companies operating in Greenland frequently cite severe logistical bottlenecks as their primary operational constraint.

The agreement emerges against a backdrop of escalating geopolitical competition. As the polar ice caps retreat, new shipping routes are opening, and the race to secure access to the Arctic seabed has intensified. Both Russia and China have expressed strong strategic interest in the region, prompting Washington to solidify its alliances with Copenhagen and the semi-autonomous government in Nuuk.

The dramatic rise in Greenland-linked equities highlights the speculative nature of frontier market investing. The current surge draws direct comparisons to August 2019 and earlier in 2026, when President Trump publicly floated the idea of the United States purchasing Greenland outright. While those proposals were swiftly rejected by Danish and Greenlandic officials, they successfully signaled to the market that Washington views the island as a paramount national security interest.

However, analysts caution that the current rally is built heavily on projection rather than immediate commercial reality. The security pact announced on Monday did not include specific commercial funding, fast-tracked mining permits, or direct subsidies for the resource sector. Companies like Greenland Mines and Critical Metals remain in the exploratory or early developmental stages, facing immense environmental and regulatory hurdles before they can achieve commercial production.

The primary economic draw of Greenland lies in its vast, largely untapped deposits of rare earth elements, uranium, and base metals. These materials are critical for the global energy transition, powering everything from electric vehicle batteries to advanced military guidance systems. Currently, global supply chains for rare earth elements are heavily dominated by China, creating an urgent accountability mandate for Western governments to secure independent supply lines.

By expanding its military footprint, the U.S. government is effectively de-risking the jurisdiction for private capital. However, the ultimate authority over resource extraction resides with the Greenlandic government in Nuuk. Local authorities must balance the promise of economic independence—fueled by mining royalties—with profound environmental concerns and the preservation of traditional Indigenous ways of life.

The intersection of military expansion and speculative mining carries profound implications for Greenland's population of roughly 56,000 people. While the influx of American capital could provide the economic foundation necessary for Greenland to pursue full independence from Denmark, it also risks overwhelming local institutions. The rapid industrialization of pristine Arctic environments remains a highly contentious domestic political issue.

For the companies whose stocks surged this week, the challenge will be translating geopolitical momentum into operational success. The harsh climate, lack of existing infrastructure, and stringent environmental regulations mean that establishing a profitable mine in Greenland requires billions of dollars in upfront capital and years of patient development.

Investors and policy analysts are now looking toward the United Nations General Assembly, where the formal signing of the pact is expected to yield specific details regarding troop deployments and infrastructure commitments. The ultimate test of Monday's market rally will be whether the U.S. government follows its military agreements with concrete financial mechanisms, such as Export-Import Bank financing, to support the commercial ambitions of the surging equities.

sources.title: Trump’s Greenland deal: How Arctic pact bolsters Golden Dome against Russia, China
passages: Trump announces agreement with Denmark to secure ‘permanent’ control over Greenland’s security.Why Greenland matters for the Golden DomeGolden Dome is Trump’s proposed multi-layered missile defence system designed to detect, track and intercept ballistic, cruise and hypersonic missiles targeting the US.

We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many,' Trump wrote while annoucing the deal.What has actually been agreedDanish prime minister Mette Frederiksen said the deal does not hand the United States sovereignty over Greenland, describing it instead an arrangement that strengthens shared security in the Arctic and North Atlantic and recognises the Greenlandic people's right to self determination.The United States, Denmark and Greenland are expected to sign the text next week at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, reported CNBC.

It has also been point out that interceptor tests over the past two decades have succeeded only about half the time, and under conditions far kinder than a real attack.Locking out Moscow and BeijingThe second purpose of the deal is to keep rivals out as Trump said no American adversary may ever build a base in Greenland, station forces there, or make sensitive investments, without express written approval from Washington.In plain terms, a Chinese state firm buying a stake in a Greenlandic mine or port would now need an American signature first.

Pituffik Space Base, formerly known as Thule, lies above the Arctic Circle roughly halfway between Washington and Moscow, and its radar can watch deep into Russia and across the likely flight paths of Chinese missiles, buying American decision makers precious extra minutes.Trump wants Golden Dome fully working by January 2029 at a cost of 175 billion dollars, a timetable and price tag that seems doubtful.
The official wording had not been released when Trump made his announcement.
The Tanbreez project in southern Greenland, now 92.5 per cent owned by Nasdaq listed Critical Metals, is the furthest along, with full construction not expected before spring 2027.

facts.text: Shares of U.S.-listed companies exposed to Greenland surged on Monday after the U.S. and Denmark reached a deal on security arrangements on the Arctic territory.

"It is joyous that we are about to make an agreement that will ensure and strengthen the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western Alliance," Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said in a statement.

The Texas-based company, which has links to Trump , recently delayed plans to drill for oil in Greenland after the island's government issued a " strong warning " to its joint venture partner for bringing equipment ashore without permission.
President Donald Trum p's threats to annex the self-governing Danish territory, with the president insisting Greenland is critical to U.S. national security.
President Donald Trump, aims to substantially expand the American military presence in the strategically vital Arctic territory.
The intersection of military expansion and speculative mining carries profound implications for Greenland's population of roughly 56,000 people.
While the influx of American capital could provide the economic foundation necessary for Greenland to pursue full independence from Denmark, it also risks overwhelming local institutions.
The rapid industrialization of pristine Arctic environments remains a highly contentious domestic political issue.

Trump announces agreement with Denmark to secure ‘permanent’ control over Greenland’s security.Why Greenland matters for the Golden DomeGolden Dome is Trump’s proposed multi-layered missile defence system designed to detect, track and intercept ballistic, cruise and hypersonic missiles targeting the US.

It has also been point out that interceptor tests over the past two decades have succeeded only about half the time, and under conditions far kinder than a real attack.Locking out Moscow and BeijingThe second purpose of the deal is to keep rivals out as Trump said no American adversary may ever build a base in Greenland, station forces there, or make sensitive investments, without express written approval from Washington.In plain terms, a Chinese state firm buying a stake in a Greenlandic mine or port would now need an American signature first.

Pituffik Space Base, formerly known as Thule, lies above the Arctic Circle roughly halfway between Washington and Moscow, and its radar can watch deep into Russia and across the likely flight paths of Chinese missiles, buying American decision makers precious extra minutes.Trump wants Golden Dome fully working by January 2029 at a cost of 175 billion dollars, a timetable and price tag that seems doubtful.
The official wording had not been released when Trump made his announcement.
The Tanbreez project in southern Greenland, now 92.5 per cent owned by Nasdaq listed Critical Metals, is the furthest along, with full construction not expected before spring 2027.

extraction.body: Shares of U.S.-listed companies exposed to Greenland surged on Monday after the U.S. and Denmark reached a deal on security arrangements on the Arctic territory. Shares of Greenland Energy soared more than 165% during premarket trading, with Greenland Mines seen up over 110% and Critical Metals Corp nearly 26% higher. The agreement, which is expected to be signed during the United Nations General Assembly this week, will see the U.S., Denmark and Greenland enter into a pact to develop a significant military presence on the territory, while blocking Washington's adversaries from building their own bases there. It follows several months of U.S. President Donald Trum p's threats to annex the self-governing Danish territory, with the president insisting Greenland is critical to U.S. national security. Announcing the deal, Trump said via Truth Social on Friday that the U.S. would "FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America." Trump said the agreement would come at no cost to the U.S., adding that Washington would "immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many." Key details of the agreement have not yet been made public. Greenlandic and Danish officials sought to reassure citizens over the weekend that the deal would respect the island's right to self-determination and the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom. "It is joyous that we are about to make an agreement that will ensure and strengthen the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western Alliance," Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said in a statement. "The agreement recognizes Greenland's interests and our place in the international cooperation. It is to the benefit of us all," he added. Greenland Energy is an oil and gas exploration firm focused on trying to unlock the hydrocarbon potential of the Jameson Land Basin on the island's east coast. The Texas-based company, which has links to Trump , recently delayed plans to drill for oil in Greenland after the island's government issued a " strong warning " to its joint venture partner for bringing equipment ashore without permission. Greenland Mines, meanwhile, is a natural resources company working on the Skaergaard Project, which ranks among the world's largest undeveloped palladium, gold and platinum deposits. Critical Metals Corp, for its part, is a mining company focused on critical metals and minerals and is developing the Tanbreez rare earths mine in southern Greenland. Got a confidential news tip? The rally followed a U.S.-Denmark-Greenland security pact aimed at expanding the military presence on the Arctic territory. Stocks of U.S.-listed companies with operational ties to Greenland experienced significant gains on Monday following the announcement of a new security agreement between the United States, Denmark, and Greenland. The trilateral pact, announced by U.S. President Donald Trump, aims to substantially expand the American military presence in the strategically vital Arctic territory. The market reaction was immediate and forceful across the basic materials sector. Shares of Greenland Energy (GLND) jumped 119 percent in extended trading, while Greenland Mines (GGRML) rose 58 percent. Critical Metals Corp (CRML) also saw a 20 percent increase. The surge reflects intense investor anticipation that the military agreement will pave the way for increased U.S. infrastructure investment and financial support for resource extraction in the region. While the diplomatic arrangement focuses explicitly on defense and preventing geopolitical adversaries from establishing Arctic bases, private capital is aggressively pricing in the secondary economic benefits of a reinforced American security umbrella. The pact is expected to be formally signed later this week during the United Nations General Assembly in New York. The new security arrangement places Arctic access at the center of U.S. foreign policy. Historically, the United States has maintained a critical strategic foothold in Greenland through the Thule Air Base—recently renamed Pituffik Space Base—which operates early warning radar systems essential for North American aerospace defense. The new pact is designed to expand this presence, allowing for greater troop deployments, maritime coordination, and shared intelligence operations. For the defense infrastructure to function effectively in the harsh Arctic environment, significant logistical upgrades are required. Military expansion inherently demands improved deep-water ports, reinforced airstrips, and robust telecommunications networks. It is this anticipated dual-use infrastructure that has galvanized the equity markets, as mining and energy companies operating in Greenland frequently cite severe logistical bottlenecks as their primary operational constraint. The agreement emerges against a backdrop of escalating geopolitical competition. As the polar ice caps retreat, new shipping routes are opening, and the race to secure access to the Arctic seabed has intensified. Both Russia and China have expressed strong strategic interest in the region, prompting Washington to solidify its alliances with Copenhagen and the semi-autonomous government in Nuuk. The dramatic rise in Greenland-linked equities highlights the speculative nature of frontier market investing. The current surge draws direct comparisons to August 2019 and earlier in 2026, when President Trump publicly floated the idea of the United States purchasing Greenland outright. While those proposals were swiftly rejected by Danish and Greenlandic officials, they successfully signaled to the market that Washington views the island as a paramount national security interest. However, analysts caution that the current rally is built heavily on projection rather than immediate commercial reality. The security pact announced on Monday did not include specific commercial funding, fast-tracked mining permits, or direct subsidies for the resource sector. Companies like Greenland Mines and Critical Metals remain in the exploratory or early developmental stages, facing immense environmental and regulatory hurdles before they can achieve commercial production. The primary economic draw of Greenland lies in its vast, largely untapped deposits of rare earth elements, uranium, and base metals. These materials are critical for the global energy transition, powering everything from electric vehicle batteries to advanced military guidance systems. Currently, global supply chains for rare earth elements are heavily dominated by China, creating an urgent accountability mandate for Western governments to secure independent supply lines. By expanding its military footprint, the U.S. government is effectively de-risking the jurisdiction for private capital. However, the ultimate authority over resource extraction resides with the Greenlandic government in Nuuk. Local authorities must balance the promise of economic independence—fueled by mining royalties—with profound environmental concerns and the preservation of traditional Indigenous ways of life. The intersection of military expansion and speculative mining carries profound implications for Greenland's population of roughly 56,000 people. While the influx of American capital could provide the economic foundation necessary for Greenland to pursue full independence from Denmark, it also risks overwhelming local institutions. The rapid industrialization of pristine Arctic environments remains a highly contentious domestic political issue. For the companies whose stocks surged this week, the challenge will be translating geopolitical momentum into operational success. The harsh climate, lack of existing infrastructure, and stringent environmental regulations mean that establishing a profitable mine in Greenland requires billions of dollars in upfront capital and years of patient development. Investors and policy analysts are now looking toward the United Nations General Assembly, where the formal signing of the pact is expected to yield specific details regarding troop deployments and infrastructure commitments. The ultimate test of Monday's market rally will be whether the U.S. government follows its military agreements with concrete financial mechanisms, such as Export-Import Bank financing, to support the commercial ambitions of the surging equities. facts.text: Shares of U.S.-listed companies exposed to Greenland surged on Monday after the U.S. and Denmark reached a deal on security arrangements on the Arctic territory.

"It is joyous that we are about to make an agreement that will ensure and strengthen the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western Alliance," Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said in a statement.

The Texas-based company, which has links to Trump , recently delayed plans to drill for oil in Greenland after the island's government issued a " strong warning " to its joint venture partner for bringing equipment ashore without permission.
President Donald Trum p's threats to annex the self-governing Danish territory, with the president insisting Greenland is critical to U.S. national security.
President Donald Trump, aims to substantially expand the American military presence in the strategically vital Arctic territory.
The intersection of military expansion and speculative mining carries profound implications for Greenland's population of roughly 56,000 people.
While the influx of American capital could provide the economic foundation necessary for Greenland to pursue full independence from Denmark, it also risks overwhelming local institutions.
The rapid industrialization of pristine Arctic environments remains a highly contentious domestic political issue.

passages: COPENHAGEN, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Denmark, Greenland and the United States are set to sign a deal on Greenland's security on Tuesday, an agreement Denmark says will put Arctic security under NATO's watch rather than leaving it solely to Washington and Copenhagen.
Denmark and Greenland have not commented on Trump's claim but said the deal will benefit the Arctic island and respect its sovereignty.

"It (the agreement) will be in a form where responsibility for security in the Arctic is not only Danish or American," Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen told national broadcaster TV2 on Sunday.
He added that to a large extent "it would be NATO that looks after the Arctic".

Erik Jensen, an opposition lawmaker in Greenland, wrote on Facebook that he had read the draft agreement: "I feel reassured and am not worried," he said, adding that the island's foreign minister was handling the work well. extraction.body: COPENHAGEN, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Denmark, Greenland and the United States are set to sign a deal on Greenland's security on Tuesday, an agreement Denmark says will put Arctic security under NATO's watch rather than leaving it solely to Washington and Copenhagen. The agreement, expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, has not been made public, though President Donald Trump says it grants the US "permanent control". Denmark and Greenland have not commented on Trump's claim but said the deal will benefit the Arctic island and respect its sovereignty. The deal follows months of pressure from Trump, who has said the United States should control Greenland and at times refused to rule out using military or economic force to acquire the semi-autonomous Danish territory. His threats, which peaked in January, triggered a diplomatic crisis within NATO and pushed Denmark and Greenland into negotiations with Washington aimed at defusing the pressure. "It (the agreement) will be in a form where responsibility for security in the Arctic is not only Danish or American," Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen told national broadcaster TV2 on Sunday. He added that to a large extent "it would be NATO that looks after the Arctic". PROMOTING 'SECURITY, STABILITY AND COOPERATION' A NATO spokesperson said on Saturday that the alliance welcomed the agreement, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region". "But we have said from the start that we are open to accommodating the United States' legitimate security interests," Rasmussen told Danish news agency Ritzau on Monday. Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Friday the agreement gives the United States "permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland," and that no US adversary could have a base or military presence there without Washington's written approval. Denmark has not responded to Trump's claim, though Copenhagen has earlier acknowledged it underinvested in Greenland's defence for decades and has pledged to expand its military presence on the island, including more NATO troops. Key details have not been made public, including whether the deal amends the 1951 defence agreement that is the legal basis for the US presence in Greenland. Greenland's government has sought to reassure the public about the deal. passages: COPENHAGEN, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Denmark, Greenland and the United States are set to sign a deal on Greenland's security on Tuesday, an agreement Denmark says will put Arctic security under NATO's watch rather than leaving it solely to Washington and Copenhagen.
The agreement, expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, has not been made public, though President Donald Trump says it grants the US "permanent control".
Denmark and Greenland have not commented on Trump's claim but said the deal will benefit the Arctic island and respect its sovereignty.

The deal follows months of pressure from Trump, who has said the United States should control Greenland and at times refused to rule out using military or economic force to acquire the semi-autonomous Danish territory.
His threats, which peaked in January, triggered a diplomatic crisis within NATO and pushed Denmark and Greenland into negotiations with Washington aimed at defusing the pressure.

"It (the agreement) will be in a form where responsibility for security in the Arctic is not only Danish or American," Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen told national broadcaster TV2 on Sunday.
He added that to a large extent "it would be NATO that looks after the Arctic".

PROMOTING 'SECURITY, STABILITY AND COOPERATION' A NATO spokesperson said on Saturday that the alliance welcomed the agreement, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region".
"But we have said from the start that we are open to accommodating the United States' legitimate security interests," Rasmussen told Danish news agency Ritzau on Monday.

Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Friday the agreement gives the United States "permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland," and that no US adversary could have a base or military presence there without Washington's written approval.

Denmark has not responded to Trump's claim, though Copenhagen has earlier acknowledged it underinvested in Greenland's defence for decades and has pledged to expand its military presence on the island, including more NATO troops.
Key details have not been made public, including whether the deal amends the 1951 defence agreement that is the legal basis for the US presence in Greenland.
Greenland's government has sought to reassure the public about the deal.

Erik Jensen, an opposition lawmaker in Greenland, wrote on Facebook that he had read the draft agreement: "I feel reassured and am not worried," he said, adding that the island's foreign minister was handling the work well. (Reporting by Stine Jacobsen and Jacob Gronholt-PedersenEditing by Gareth Jones) By Stine Jacobsen and Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen

Speaking to DW on Monday, Kofod looked back on how he worked with the first Trump administration, with Mike Pompeo as US Secretary of State, to appease Trump the first time he floated the idea of buying Greenland during his first term in office. The former foreign minister, who is now CEO of consulting company Kofod Global, noted the Danish investment in Greenland in recent years, contrasting it against what he said was a US scale back of investment. "Denmark has [in] recent years put more troops in Greenland, more military assets. And alongside other NATO countries, we are, as we speak, deploying much more assets to the High North and Greenland," he noted. Meanwhile, he argued, the US "in the last decades has really, really scaled back." "I mean, when there was most troops and soldiers, military staff from the US, this was around 10,000 in the high days of the Cold War, maybe 15 to 17 bases in Greenland, US bases. Now they're down to one military base, space base and only 150 troops. So [the] US has not prioritized to put more troops in Greenland," Kofod said. Kofod reiterated warnings that the NATO alliance would come to an end should Trump deliver on his threat. He said if the US were to take Greenland against the will of fellow NATO member Denmark, "that will be the end of NATO and it will lead to open conflict over the Atlantic between all of Europe and [the] United States and also [the] United States and most of the rest of the world."
